title: Metabolism: how your cells break food down, build you up and keep you warm

summary.text: A tumbler of warm water left on the table is cool within the hour. Your body has stayed warm for years, day and night, with no stove inside it. Where does the warmth come from? In this lesson you feed living yeast four different foods and measure the gas they make. You find out what a cell does with food: it breaks some of it down for energy, and uses that energy to build and repair the body. Heat escapes at every step, and that is why you are warm, and a little warmer after a meal.
summary.art: A steel tumbler of water cooling on a table beside a child holding a palm to their own warm cheek, with four small bottles topped by balloons of different sizes in the background.

intro.hook: Put your palm on your cheek. It is warm. It was warm while you slept last night, and it will be warm tomorrow. A tumbler of warm water goes cool in an hour. So why do you never go cool?
intro.text: Say what you think, and why. Then try the first activity, Warmer Than the Room. You will set a tumbler of warm water beside you and see which of you stays warm. After that you will feed yeast, who are tiny living beings, and see what they do with food. By the end you will know where your warmth comes from. You will also know why a meal makes you feel warmer.
intro.art: A child sitting at a table with one palm on a cheek, looking at a steel tumbler of water with a little steam above it, and a question mark between the two.

outcomes: By the end I can say what metabolism is, and tell breaking down (catabolism) from building up (anabolism).
By the end I can explain why my cells can build only with energy from breaking food down, and say what ATP does.
By the end I can explain where body heat comes from, and why I feel warmer after a meal.
By the end I can say which parts of a resting body use the most energy.
By the end I can explain how the body stores energy as glycogen and fat, and when it uses each store.
By the end I can say where the atoms of my food end up: built into my body, or breathed out.
By the end I can run a fair test with living yeast and explain the result with a claim, evidence and reasoning.
By the end I can compare how fast different animals use energy, and say why a small animal must eat so often.

terms.meaning: Metabolism is all the chemical changes that go on inside the cells of a living being. Some changes break molecules down, and others build new molecules.
terms.example: Right now your cells are breaking down sugar from your last meal and building new skin, both at once.
terms.art: A cell drawn as a busy workshop, with large molecules being taken apart on one side and new ones being put together on the other.

terms.meaning: A molecule is a group of atoms joined together. Sugar, water, fat and protein are all made of molecules.
terms.example: One molecule of glucose has 6 carbon atoms, 12 hydrogen atoms and 6 oxygen atoms.
terms.art: A small model of a glucose molecule made of joined balls in three colours.

terms.meaning: Catabolism is the part of metabolism that breaks large molecules into smaller ones. Breaking them down releases energy.
terms.example: Your muscle cells break glucose down into carbon dioxide and water, and get energy to move.
terms.art: A large molecule splitting into small pieces, with small arrows of energy coming out.

terms.meaning: Anabolism is the part of metabolism that joins small molecules into larger ones. Building them up costs energy.
terms.example: Your body joins amino acids from dal into the protein of a new muscle fibre.
terms.art: Small pieces being joined into a long chain, with small arrows of energy going in.

terms.meaning: Glucose is a simple sugar. It is the main fuel that blood carries to your cells.
terms.example: The starch in rice and idli is cut into glucose in your gut, and the glucose passes into your blood.
terms.art: A bowl of rice with an arrow to a chain of beads, and an arrow from the chain to single beads labelled glucose.

terms.meaning: ATP is a small molecule that carries energy inside a cell. Its full name is adenosine triphosphate. A cell loads ATP with energy when it breaks food down, and spends ATP wherever it needs energy.
terms.example: A muscle fibre spends ATP each time it shortens. A cell also spends ATP to join amino acids into protein.
terms.art: A small molecule drawn like a loaded spring moving from a 'breaking down' corner of a cell to a 'building' corner.

terms.meaning: Cellular respiration is the way a cell breaks glucose or fat down with oxygen. It gives carbon dioxide, water and energy. It is not the same as breathing, which only moves air in and out.
terms.example: You breathe faster when you run, because your muscle cells are using more oxygen for cellular respiration.
terms.art: A cell with glucose and oxygen going in, and carbon dioxide, water and energy coming out.

terms.meaning: Fermentation is a way of getting energy from sugar without oxygen. It breaks the sugar only part of the way, so it gives much less energy.
terms.example: Yeast in idli or bread dough ferment sugar and give off carbon dioxide gas, which makes the dough rise.
terms.art: A covered vessel of batter risen to the rim with bubbles in it.

terms.meaning: A mitochondrion is a small part inside a cell where food is broken down with oxygen. The plural is mitochondria. Most of a cell's ATP is loaded there.
terms.example: A heart muscle cell is packed with mitochondria, because the heart never rests.
terms.art: A cell cut open to show many small bean-shaped parts with folded insides.

terms.meaning: Metabolic rate is how fast a body uses energy. It can be given in kilocalories a day or in watts.
terms.example: Your metabolic rate goes up many times when you run, and falls again when you sit.
terms.art: A child running with a large flame symbol and the same child sitting with a small flame symbol.

terms.meaning: Basal metabolic rate is the energy a body uses while lying awake, at rest, in a comfortable room, long after a meal. It is the cost of only staying alive.
terms.example: Even when you lie still, your heart, brain, liver and kidneys keep working and using energy.
terms.art: A child lying awake and still on a mat, with the heart, brain, liver and kidneys shown glowing.

terms.meaning: The thermic effect of food is the extra energy a body uses to digest, absorb and store a meal. That extra energy ends up as heat.
terms.example: For an hour or more after a big lunch your body gives off a little more heat than before it.
terms.art: A child after a meal with small heat waves rising from the body and an empty banana leaf in front.

terms.meaning: Glycogen is a store of glucose. It is made of many glucose units joined in a branching chain, and it is kept in the liver and the muscles.
terms.example: During the night your liver breaks glycogen back into glucose, so your brain has fuel while you sleep.
terms.art: A branching chain of beads inside a liver, with single beads leaving into a blood vessel.

terms.meaning: Body fat is the body's large, long-lasting store of energy. It is kept in fat cells under the skin and around the organs.
terms.example: A bar-headed goose builds up body fat before flying over the Himalayas, and uses it on the way.
terms.art: A goose in flight with a small store symbol on the body getting smaller along the route.

terms.meaning: Brown fat is a special kind of fat whose cells break fuel down only to make heat. Babies have a good deal of it, and adults have a little.
terms.example: A newborn baby cannot shiver well, so brown fat near the neck and back helps keep the baby warm.
terms.art: A sleeping newborn baby with warm patches shown at the back of the neck and between the shoulders.

terms.meaning: Turnover is the steady breaking down and rebuilding of the body's own molecules. The body looks the same, but its material keeps being replaced.
terms.example: A red blood cell lasts about four months. Then it is taken apart, and a new one takes its place.
terms.art: A wall in which old bricks are being taken out at one end while new bricks are put in at the other, so the wall keeps its shape.

terms.meaning: Lactate is a small molecule that muscle cells make when they break glucose down very fast. It is a fuel. The heart burns it, and the liver builds it back into glucose.
terms.example: After a hard sprint your blood carries extra lactate from your leg muscles to your liver.
terms.art: An arrow from a leg muscle to the liver labelled lactate, and an arrow back labelled glucose.

terms.meaning: A watt is a unit for how fast energy is used or given out. One watt is one joule of energy every second.
terms.example: A resting ten-year-old gives out heat at about 55 watts, a little less than an old 60 watt bulb.
terms.art: A resting child and a glowing light bulb side by side with similar small heat waves.

terms.meaning: Torpor is a state in which an animal lets their body cool and their metabolic rate fall very low for some hours, to save energy.
terms.example: Some bats and hummingbirds go into torpor when they rest, because their small bodies would otherwise run out of fuel.
terms.art: A small bat hanging asleep with a tiny flame symbol, beside the same bat flying with a large flame symbol.

explanations.concept: Metabolism: the chemistry that keeps a cell alive
explanations.definition: Metabolism is all the chemical changes inside the cells of a living being. It has two parts. Catabolism breaks molecules down, and anabolism builds molecules up.
explanations.description: Digestion happens in the gut, which is a tube. Metabolism happens later, inside your cells, after the digested food has crossed into the blood. A cell takes in small molecules such as glucose, fatty acids and amino acids. Then it does one of two things with each of them. It can break the molecule down further and take the energy. Or it can join the molecule to others and build something the body needs. Thousands of different changes go on in one cell at the same time. Each change is helped by its own enzyme. An enzyme is a protein that makes one chemical change happen quickly at body warmth. Every living cell has a metabolism: yours, a neem tree's, a yeast cell's and a bacterium's. When metabolism stops for good, the cell has died.
examples: Glucose from your breakfast idli is broken down in a leg muscle cell, and the muscle uses the energy to climb stairs.
Amino acids from sambar dal are joined into the protein of a new skin cell where you grazed your knee.
In the Yeast Fuel Test, yeast cells break sugar down, and you catch the gas they give off in a balloon.
explanations.art: A cell with small molecules coming in from a blood vessel, some going to a 'break down' side and some to a 'build up' side.

explanations.definition: Catabolism is the breaking of large molecules into smaller ones. It releases energy that was stored in the food molecule.
explanations.description: A glucose molecule holds energy in the way its atoms are joined. You saw this energy in Class 4, when a burning groundnut warmed water. A cell does not burn glucose in one go. It takes the molecule apart in more than twenty small steps, and each step has its own enzyme. In the end the carbon atoms leave as carbon dioxide, and the hydrogen atoms join oxygen and leave as water. This whole path is cellular respiration, and most of it happens in the mitochondria. Why so many steps? A single big step would let all the energy out as heat at once. Small steps let the cell catch part of the energy each time, in ATP. Fat and protein can be broken down for energy too. Fat gives the most energy for each gram.
examples: Cells in your heart break down fat and lactate all day to keep the heart beating.
When you run for a bus, your leg muscles break glucose down many times faster than when you sit.
A camel's hump is fat. Over days without food, the camel's cells break that fat down for energy.
explanations.art: A glucose molecule passing down a staircase of small steps, with a little energy caught at each step, and carbon dioxide and water at the bottom.

explanations.definition: Anabolism is the joining of small molecules into larger ones. It costs energy. In your body that energy comes from catabolism.
explanations.description: Your body is built from the same kinds of small molecules that digestion gives you. Amino acids are joined into proteins, such as the fibres of muscle and the enzymes in every cell. Glucose units are joined into glycogen. Fatty acids are joined into fats and into the thin skin around each cell. None of these joins happens by itself. Each one needs energy, and the cell pays with ATP. So building depends on breaking. A child who is growing does a great deal of anabolism. An adult who has stopped growing still does a great deal, because the body rebuilds itself all the time. Plants do anabolism too. A rice plant joins carbon dioxide and water into glucose, using the energy of light, and then joins glucose into starch.
examples: After you graze your knee, cells at the edge of the cut build new protein and new cells to close it.
At night, when you are growing, your bones add new material at their growing ends.
In Grown in the Dark, a moong seedling builds a root and a shoot with energy from breaking down the food stored in the seed.
explanations.art: Loose amino acids being joined into a long folded chain inside a cell, with small ATP symbols being used up at each join.

explanations.concept: ATP carries energy from the breaking to the building
explanations.definition: ATP is a small molecule that carries energy inside a cell. Catabolism loads it with energy, and anabolism and every other job in the cell spend it.
explanations.description: Breaking down and building up happen in different places in a cell, and at different moments. Something has to carry the energy from one to the other. That carrier is ATP. When a cell breaks glucose down, it uses the energy to load ATP. When the cell needs energy, it spends an ATP. The spent molecule is called ADP, and it goes back to be loaded again. The same ATP molecule is loaded and spent again and again, many hundreds of times a day. Teachers often say that an adult loads and spends about their own body weight of ATP each day. That number is a rough estimate, not a measurement. ATP was found in 1929. Yellapragada SubbaRow, who was born in Bhimavaram in Andhra Pradesh, and Cyrus Fiske found it in the United States. Karl Lohmann found it in Germany in the same year. All known living cells use ATP.
examples: A nerve cell in your brain spends ATP to pump charged atoms across its skin, so that it is ready to send the next signal.
A yeast cell loads ATP by fermenting sugar, and spends ATP to grow and divide.
A firefly spends ATP to make light.
explanations.art: A loop with ATP being loaded at a mitochondrion and spent at a muscle fibre and at a protein being built, then returning as ADP.

explanations.concept: Why every step gives off heat
explanations.definition: No change of energy from one form to another is complete. Each time a cell loads ATP or spends ATP, part of the energy escapes as heat.
explanations.description: When a cell breaks glucose down with oxygen, it catches roughly 35 to 40 parts in every 100 of the energy in ATP. The other 60 or more parts become heat at once. Then the ATP is spent. Whatever it is spent on, that energy also ends as heat inside you, unless you do work on something outside your body or store the energy in new body material. A beating heart pushes blood, and the blood rubs against the vessel walls and warms them. So a body at rest gives out, as heat, all the energy it uses. For a resting ten-year-old that is about 55 watts. For a resting adult it is about 80 watts. Your body cannot switch this heat off. Most of it is not made on purpose. It comes with being alive. Shivering and brown fat are the body's two ways of making extra heat on purpose. Mammals and birds keep much of it in with fur, feathers and fat, and so stay warm.
examples: A crowded bus feels warm even on a cool morning, because every passenger gives out heat all the time.
Your phone grows warm when it works hard, for the same reason: no machine passes energy on completely.
In Warmer Than the Room, the tumbler of water goes cool and you stay warm, because you keep making heat and the water does not.
explanations.art: A glucose molecule with 100 units of energy, an arrow of about 40 units going to ATP and an arrow of about 60 units leaving as heat waves.

explanations.concept: Why you feel warm after eating
explanations.definition: After a meal your body uses extra energy to digest the food, carry it across the gut wall and store it. This extra use is called the thermic effect of food, and it ends as extra heat.
explanations.description: A meal makes work for your cells. Gut muscles squeeze the food along. Gland cells build and send out enzymes. Cells in the gut wall spend ATP to pull glucose and amino acids into the blood. Liver and muscle cells spend ATP to join glucose into glycogen and to build proteins. All this spending gives off heat. For a mixed meal, the extra energy used is about one tenth of the energy in the meal. Protein costs the most to handle, carbohydrate less, and fat the least. These shares are rough, because they are hard to measure. Your body temperature hardly changes after a meal. The brain notices the extra heat and sends more blood to the skin, so the heat leaves. That is why your skin, more than your insides, feels warmer. Three other things can add to the feeling. Hot food and drink carry their own heat into you. Chilli contains capsaicin, which switches on the nerve endings that sense heat, so you feel hot although nothing has warmed up. And your heart beats a little faster after a meal, to send more blood to the gut.
examples: After a wedding lunch on a banana leaf, many people feel warm and sleepy for an hour or two.
A Burmese python may eat a meal a quarter of their own weight or more. Their metabolic rate can then rise to as much as 44 times its resting level.
In the Lunch Test you count your pulse and take your temperature before and after a meal.
explanations.art: A child after lunch with arrows showing blood flowing to the gut and to the skin, and small heat waves leaving the skin.

explanations.concept: Basal metabolic rate: what a resting body spends energy on
explanations.definition: Basal metabolic rate is the energy a body uses while lying awake and at rest, in a comfortable room, many hours after a meal. For most people it is well over half of all the energy they use in a day.
explanations.description: A resting body is busy. The heart beats, the kidneys clean the blood, the liver runs hundreds of chemical changes, and the brain never switches off. In an adult, four organs do more than half of this resting work: the liver, the brain, the heart and the kidneys. Together they are only about one twentieth of the body's weight. The brain is about 2 parts in 100 of an adult's weight, and uses about 20 parts in 100 of the resting energy. Muscles at rest use little for their size, but there is so much muscle that it adds up to about a fifth. In a child the brain's share is far bigger. A study in 2014 worked out that a child's brain, at four to five years old, uses glucose at a rate equal to about two thirds of the body's resting energy. The same study found that the body grows most slowly at the ages when the brain uses most. Basal metabolic rate depends mostly on body size and on how much of the body is muscle and organs.
examples: While you sleep, your body still uses energy at nearly its basal rate.
In Twenty Beans you guess where a resting body spends its energy, and then compare with the measurements.
A person with fever has a higher metabolic rate, because chemical changes go faster in a warmer body.
explanations.art: An outline of a resting adult body with the brain, liver, heart and kidneys coloured strongly and the muscles coloured faintly.

explanations.definition: The body stores spare energy in two main forms. Glycogen is a small, quick store of glucose in the liver and the muscles. Fat is a large, slow store in fat cells.
explanations.description: You eat a few times a day, but your cells need fuel every second. Stores fill the gaps. After a meal, the liver and the muscles join spare glucose into glycogen. This is anabolism. Between meals and at night, the liver breaks glycogen back into glucose and lets it out into the blood. This is catabolism. An adult's liver holds about 100 grams of glycogen, and the muscles hold about 400 grams. Muscle glycogen is used only by the muscle that holds it. Glycogen holds water around it, so it is heavy for the energy it gives. Fat holds no water and gives more than twice the energy for each gram, so the body keeps its big store as fat. Gerty Cori and Carl Cori worked out how the body builds glycogen and breaks it down. In 1929 they also described what is now called the Cori cycle. A hard-working muscle breaks glucose down to lactate. The blood carries the lactate to the liver, and the liver builds it back into glucose. So lactate is a fuel being passed on. It is not a poison.
examples: A marathon runner who runs out of glycogen suddenly feels very weak. Runners call this 'hitting the wall'.
A Himalayan brown bear eats through summer and autumn, and lives on body fat while sleeping through the winter.
During an overnight fast your liver glycogen keeps the glucose in your blood steady until breakfast.
explanations.art: A liver and a leg muscle each holding a small branching store, and fat cells under the skin holding a large store, with arrows to and from the blood.

explanations.concept: Turnover: your body is rebuilt all the time
explanations.definition: Turnover is the steady breaking down and rebuilding of the body's own molecules and cells. It goes on in everybody, including adults who are no longer growing.
explanations.description: It is natural to think that food is fuel and the body is the engine, and that the engine's parts stay the same for years. Tests with labelled atoms in the 1930s showed that this is wrong. The body takes its own proteins and fats apart all the time, and builds new ones from a mix of old pieces and new food. An adult breaks down and rebuilds about 300 grams of protein every day. That is three or four times the protein the adult eats. A red blood cell lasts about four months. The cells that line the small intestine last only a few days. Why would a body do this? Proteins get damaged, and a damaged enzyme works badly. Rebuilding keeps the parts fresh. It also lets the body change quickly, by building more of one protein and less of another. Not everything is replaced. Most nerve cells in the brain last a lifetime, and so does the hard enamel of your teeth.
examples: The skin you can see today is not the skin you had two months ago. The outer cells have been shed and replaced.
A broken arm in a cast gets thinner in a few weeks. Muscle protein is still being broken down, and less is being rebuilt.
A healing bone is first joined by rough new bone, which is then taken apart and rebuilt into its proper shape.
explanations.art: A human outline made of small tiles, with old tiles leaving on one side and new tiles arriving from a plate of food on the other.

explanations.concept: Where the atoms of your food go
explanations.definition: Atoms are never destroyed in the body. The atoms of food that is broken down for energy leave mostly as carbon dioxide in the breath and as water.
explanations.description: Glucose and fat are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms. When a cell breaks them down fully, each carbon atom leaves joined to oxygen, as carbon dioxide. Your blood carries that gas to your lungs, and you breathe it out. The hydrogen atoms end up in water, which leaves in urine, sweat and breath. So when a person's body uses up 10 kilograms of stored fat, about 8.4 kilograms of it leave through the lungs as carbon dioxide. The other 1.6 kilograms leave as water. Two scientists in Australia, Ruben Meerman and Andrew Brown, worked this out in 2014. They also found that most doctors they asked got it wrong. Many thought the fat turned into energy or heat. But atoms cannot turn into energy in a body. The energy comes from the way the atoms were joined, and the atoms themselves go on. Protein also contains nitrogen. The liver puts that nitrogen into urea, and the kidneys send the urea out in urine.
examples: You weigh a little less in the morning than at bedtime. Part of the difference is carbon you breathed out in the night, and part is water.
A carbon atom you breathe out today may be taken in by a tulsi leaf tomorrow and built into sugar.
A candle gets shorter as it burns, because its wax leaves as carbon dioxide and water vapour.
explanations.art: A fat cell with arrows showing most of its atoms leaving through the lungs as carbon dioxide and a smaller share leaving as water drops.

explanations.concept: With oxygen and without: respiration and fermentation
explanations.definition: A cell can break glucose down fully, using oxygen, or only part of the way, without oxygen. The first way is cellular respiration. The second is fermentation, and it gives much less energy.
explanations.description: The first part of breaking down glucose is a path of ten steps called glycolysis. It needs no oxygen, and it loads only a little ATP. Nearly every living cell has this same path, from bacteria to yeast to you. That is strong evidence that all life shares one ancestor. After glycolysis there is a choice. With oxygen, your mitochondria break the pieces down all the way to carbon dioxide and water. This loads about fifteen times as much ATP as glycolysis alone. Without oxygen, a yeast cell turns the pieces into alcohol and carbon dioxide. That is fermentation. Most of the energy stays in the alcohol, so the yeast must use a lot of sugar. Your own muscle cells do something similar in a hard sprint. They turn the pieces into lactate, which other cells burn later. In the Yeast Fuel Test the bottles are closed with balloons, so the yeast soon have little oxygen and they ferment.
examples: Idli and dosa batter rises overnight because bacteria and wild yeasts in it ferment sugars and give off carbon dioxide.
A 100 metre sprinter gets much of her energy without oxygen for those few seconds, and breathes hard afterwards.
Yeast given air and stirred well use oxygen and grow faster on the same sugar.
explanations.art: One glucose molecule at the top of a path that forks: one branch with oxygen ends in carbon dioxide, water and many ATP, and the other ends in alcohol, carbon dioxide and few ATP.

explanations.concept: Metabolic rate in other animals, and in a flower
explanations.definition: Different living beings use energy at very different rates. For each kilogram of body, a small warm animal uses energy much faster than a large one.
explanations.description: A small body has a lot of skin for its weight, so it loses heat quickly. To stay warm, each gram of a small mammal or bird must make more heat. The Etruscan shrew weighs about 2 grams and is one of the smallest mammals. They eat one and a half to two times their own weight in food every day. An elephant eats far more in total, but far less for each kilogram of body. Animals who do not keep a steady warmth, such as snakes, frogs and fish, need much less food. A python can go weeks between meals. Some small animals save fuel by going into torpor when they rest. Honey bees keep warm together. In cold weather the bees pack into a ball and shiver their flight muscles without moving their wings. The heat comes from the honey they eat. Some plants make heat too. The flower of the sacred lotus keeps itself at about 30 to 35 degrees Celsius for a few days, even when the air is as cool as 10 degrees. Lotus cells do this by breaking down stored food very fast.
examples: A sunbird at a hibiscus must feed again and again through the day, because a small warm body uses fuel quickly.
A rock python lying still after a meal is not being lazy. Their body is working hard on the meal.
On a cool morning, a lotus flower in a temple tank can be several degrees warmer than the air around it.
explanations.art: A tiny shrew beside a heap of insects twice their size, an elephant beside a small heap of grass for their size, and a lotus flower with a thermometer reading warmer than the air.

explanations.concept: Why does metabolic rate change with body size in the way it does?
explanations.description: An elephant weighs about a million times as much as a small shrew, but uses far less than a million times the energy. In 1932 Max Kleiber measured many mammals. He found that when body weight goes up 10,000 times, metabolic rate goes up only about 1,000 times. This pattern is called Kleiber's law. Scientists agree on the pattern in a rough way. They do not agree on why it happens, or on how exact it is.
examples: A mouse's heart beats about 600 times a minute, and an elephant's about 30 times.
A gram of shrew uses energy many times faster than a gram of elephant.

perspectives.explanation: A body loses heat through its skin. A big body has less skin for its weight, so it needs less heat for each kilogram. This explains part of the pattern, but the numbers do not fit it exactly.

perspectives.who: Geoffrey West, James Brown and Brian Enquist (1997)
perspectives.explanation: Every cell is fed through branching tubes, such as blood vessels. In a bigger body the tubes are longer, and that limits how fast fuel can be delivered to each cell. Their sums give the pattern Kleiber found.
There is no single law. Careful measurements give different patterns for small animals and large ones, and for resting and active animals. So there may be several causes working together.

explanations.art: A row of animals from a shrew to an elephant, each with a flame showing total energy use growing more slowly than body size.

explanations.concept: Does a more active person always use more energy in a day?
explanations.description: It seems obvious that someone who moves more uses more energy in total. For a single day that is true. Over months, the measurements are less clear, and scientists disagree about what they mean. Moving your body is good for your heart, muscles, bones and mood, whichever side turns out to be right.
examples: A child who plays football for an hour uses more energy in that hour than a child who reads.

perspectives.explanation: They measured the Hadza people of Tanzania, who walk many kilometres a day to find food. For their body size, the Hadza used about the same energy each day as office workers in cities. Pontzer thinks the body keeps its daily total within limits, and saves on other jobs when a person moves a lot.

They point out that the result depends on how body size is allowed for. Many studies show that energy use does rise with activity. They think any saving is small, and that it appears only at very high levels of activity.

explanations.art: Two people of the same size, one walking through grassland with a bow and one sitting at a desk, with similar-sized flames above them and a question mark between.

explanations.concept: Which came first when life began: metabolism or genes?
explanations.description: Every cell today has both a metabolism and genes, and each needs the other. Genes carry the plans for enzymes, and enzymes are needed to copy genes. So which came first, about four billion years ago? Nobody knows. Some scientists think simple chains of chemical changes began first, perhaps in warm, mineral-rich vents on the sea floor, and that genes came later. Others think molecules that could copy themselves came first, and that metabolism grew up around them. These are ideas, and tests are still going on.
examples: The ten steps of glycolysis are found in nearly all living beings, so that path must be very old.
Some of the steps of metabolism can be made to happen in a laboratory with only water, iron and simple molecules, with no enzymes at all.
explanations.art: A sea-floor vent with warm water rising through rock chimneys, and simple molecules joining in tiny pores in the rock.

agreed.text: Every living cell has a metabolism. It breaks some molecules down for energy and builds others up.
agreed.evidence: Wherever biologists have looked, from bacteria to banyan trees to people, they have found cells taking in molecules, changing them and giving off waste and heat.

agreed.text: Energy is neither made nor lost in a living body. The energy in the food a body uses equals the heat it gives out, plus the work it does, plus what it stores.
agreed.evidence: In the 1890s Wilbur Atwater and Edward Rosa kept people for days inside a sealed room that measured all their heat. The energy going in and the energy coming out matched very closely.

agreed.text: A body's own molecules are broken down and rebuilt all the time, even in an adult who is not growing.
agreed.evidence: From 1935, Rudolf Schoenheimer and David Rittenberg fed animals food made with labelled atoms. The labels soon turned up in the animals' own fat and protein.

agreed.text: All known living cells carry energy in the same molecule, ATP.
agreed.evidence: ATP was found in muscle in 1929. Since then it has been found in every kind of cell that has been tested.

agreed.text: Nearly all living beings break glucose down by the same first ten steps.
agreed.evidence: The enzymes for these steps have been found in bacteria, yeast, plants and animals, and they are built in closely matching ways.

agreed.text: Fat that the body uses up leaves mostly through the lungs, as carbon dioxide.
agreed.evidence: Counting the atoms in a fat molecule shows where each must go. Tests with labelled atoms agree with the count.

challenging.claim: Food is fuel and the body is an engine. The fuel is burned, and the engine's own parts stay the same for years.
challenging.for: It fits what we see. A grown person looks the same from month to month, and food clearly gives energy.
challenging.against: Labelled atoms from food turn up in body fat and body protein within days, even in adult animals who are not growing. The body is taken apart and rebuilt all the time.
challenging.context: This card is about an old picture of the body: an engine that only burns its food.

challenging.for: Heat escapes at every step of metabolism whether the body wants it or not. A lizard's body makes heat too, though far less, and it is not enough to keep the lizard warm.
challenging.against: Mammals and birds depend on this heat to stay at a steady warmth. Brown fat cells break fuel down only to make heat. So the same heat is waste in one body and a need in another.
challenging.context: This card is about the heat that metabolism gives off. Is it waste, or something the body uses?

challenging.claim: Lactic acid builds up in tired muscles and causes the soreness you feel the next day.
challenging.for: Muscles do make more lactate during hard exercise, and hard exercise is followed by soreness.
challenging.against: Lactate is cleared from the blood within about an hour, long before the soreness starts. It is a fuel that the heart burns and the liver builds back into glucose. Next-day soreness comes from tiny damage to muscle fibres and the repair that follows.
challenging.context: This card is about lactate, which muscles make when they break glucose down very fast.

challenging.claim: A growing body makes order out of disorder, so living beings break the rule that things get more mixed up over time.
challenging.who: A puzzle that physicists raised, and Erwin Schrödinger wrote about in 1944
challenging.for: A baby builds a neat, working body out of mashed food. That looks like order appearing from disorder.
challenging.against: A body builds its order only by giving out heat and simple waste molecules, such as carbon dioxide. These spread out and add more disorder outside the body than the order built inside. So the rule holds.
challenging.context: This card is about a rule of physics: left alone, things get more mixed up. Does a growing body break it?

challenging.claim: Mitochondria were once free-living bacteria, which came to live inside larger cells.
challenging.for: Mitochondria have their own small ring of genes, like bacteria. They divide by themselves, and they are the size of bacteria.
challenging.against: At first most biologists did not accept it, and about fifteen journals turned her paper down. Later, the genes of mitochondria were read and found to match those of one group of bacteria.
challenging.context: This card is about where mitochondria came from. They are the parts of a cell that break food down with oxygen.

big_questions.q: Your cells can build only by breaking food down. Can any living being grow without something being taken apart?
big_questions.hint: Think of the moong seedling in the dark, a calf drinking milk, and a rice plant in sunlight.

big_questions.q: Most of the protein in your body is replaced within months. What stays the same, so that you are still you?
big_questions.hint: Think of a river, or a school that keeps its name while the children change every year.

big_questions.q: This morning's idli is now partly your arm and partly your breath. Where does the meal end and you begin?
big_questions.hint: Is there a moment when a glucose molecule stops being food and becomes you?

big_questions.q: Yeast and you break glucose down by the same first ten steps. What does that tell you about yeast and you?
big_questions.hint: How could two such different beings come to have the same ten steps?

big_questions.q: A flame takes in fuel and oxygen, and gives out heat, carbon dioxide and water. So do you. Why is a flame not alive?
big_questions.hint: What does your body do with energy that a flame never does?

big_questions.q: All the energy you use ends up as heat in the air. Did you use it up, or did it only pass through you?
big_questions.hint: Where was that energy before it was in your food? Where does the heat go next?

story.title: The Kid Who Would Not Warm
story.note: Thenmozhi, Kathir, Paatti, the doctor and the goats are made up. These facts are real. Villages around Kotagiri in the Nilgiris get frost on some January nights. A newborn goat kid is born wet and loses heat fast. The kid has a small store of brown fat, which makes heat for the first hours, and needs the mother's first milk, called colostrum, soon after birth. People who keep goats are told to dry a chilled kid, warm the kid, and feed warm colostrum once the kid can swallow. A kid whose mouth feels cold must be warmed before feeding, and needs a vet.
text: The frost came on the night Paatti was away.

She had gone down to Coonoor for a wedding. Thenmozhi, who was eleven, was in charge of the house, her brother Kathir and the goats. The house stood above the tea slopes near Kotagiri. Kathir was seven and did not think he needed anyone in charge.
At two in the morning Karuppi began to call from the shed. Thenmozhi woke at once. She knew that sound. Karuppi was having her kids.

By the time the two children reached the shed with the lantern, the first kid was already out. She was black like her mother, and she was trying to stand on four legs that would not agree with one another. Karuppi was licking her hard.
"There is another," said Thenmozhi.
The second kid lay behind Karuppi in the straw. She was smaller, and brown, and still wet. She did not try to stand. Karuppi had not turned round to her yet.
Kathir touched the small kid's ear. "She is cold, Akka. She is as cold as the tap."
"Then we warm her," said Thenmozhi.
Kathir ran to the house and came back with Paatti's brown shawl. He wrapped the kid in it. They waited. Outside, the grass was turning white.
After ten minutes the kid was no warmer. Kathir fetched a blanket, and then a second blanket. Now the kid was a small face in a great heap of wool. Her eyes were half shut.
"More," said Kathir. "We need more blankets. Blankets make you warm."

Thenmozhi was not listening. She was looking at a steel tumbler on the shed step. An hour ago, before she slept, she had filled it with hot water for herself. Then she had wrapped it in her muffler and forgotten it. She picked it up. The muffler was still tight around it. The water inside was cold.
She held the tumbler and thought.

The muffler had not kept the water hot. It had only made the water cool more slowly. Wool makes no heat. Wool keeps in heat that something else is making. She herself was warm inside her sweater, because something in her was making heat all night. The tumbler had nothing in it making heat. So it had gone cold, muffler or no muffler.
She looked at the kid in the heap of blankets.
"Kathir," she said, "a blanket is no use unless there is a fire under it. Her fire is nearly out."
"Goats do not have fires."
"Everybody has one. Yours is burning your dinner right now. That is why your hands are warm. She has never had a dinner. She was born with a little fuel, and the cold is using it up."

Paatti had the vet's number written on the wall by the door. Dr Revathy answered on the sixth ring, with sleep in her voice, and woke up fast. "Is the kid wet? Dry her first. Rub her hard with a dry cloth. A wet coat steals heat. Then put your finger in her mouth. Tell me if her mouth is warm or cold."

Thenmozhi rubbed the kid with an old towel until the brown coat stood up in tufts. She slid a finger into the small mouth. It was warm. Not very warm, but warm. The kid's tongue curled weakly round her finger.
"Warm. And she is sucking my finger."

"Good. Then she can swallow. She needs her mother's first milk, and she needs it now. Milk a little into a clean tumbler and give it with a spoon, slowly, a few drops at a time. Keep her against your own body under the blanket while you do it. Call me again in half an hour."

Karuppi did not like being milked by a child at two in the morning. But Thenmozhi had done it before, and she got half a tumbler of the first milk. It was thick and yellow, more like thin payasam than milk. She sat down in the straw with the kid inside her sweater and the blankets over them both. Kathir held the tumbler.
A few drops went in. The kid swallowed. A few more.
"Now you teach me," said Kathir. "Why milk? Why not just you? You are warm."
"I am helping. My heat is going into her. But I cannot hold her for ever. She has to make her own. For that she needs fuel inside her, and this is fuel."
They gave the milk one small spoon at a time. It took a long while. The lantern hissed. The frost thickened on the tea bushes below the shed.
Then the kid began to shake.
Kathir nearly dropped the tumbler. "Akka! She is getting worse!"
Thenmozhi put her hand on the small ribs. The shaking was fast and steady, and under it the kid's skin was warmer than before.
"No," she said slowly. "She is shivering. She could not even shiver before. Her muscles are working very fast, and the work makes heat. She is burning her dinner, Kathir. Her first one."

When they called Dr Revathy again, the kid was trying to climb out of the sweater. The doctor laughed. "Put her by her mother and let her find the milk herself. I will come up in the morning to look at them both."
The brown kid stood, fell, and stood again. She pushed under Karuppi, next to her black sister, and found what she wanted. Her tail began to flick.
Kathir folded Paatti's shawl. He looked at it for a moment.
"It did help a bit," he said.
"It helped," said Thenmozhi. "Once there was something under it to keep."
story.epiphany: For the parent: a blanket, a shawl or a muffler makes no heat. It only slows the heat leaving. A living body is warm because its cells break food down all the time, and heat escapes at every step. The newborn kid had almost no fuel, so wrapping alone could not warm her. Drying her, lending her warmth and feeding her gave her own cells something to break down. Her shivering was her muscles using that fuel to make heat.
ask: A warm tumbler wrapped in wool still goes cold. A child wrapped in wool stays warm. What is the difference between them?
Why can a newborn animal get cold much faster than a grown one?
Shivering looks like a bad sign. Why can it be a good one?
What three things warmed the kid, and what did each one do?
Where does your own warmth come from on a cold night?

games.title: Break or Build?
games.context: This is a card game about the two halves of metabolism. Each card describes something a living body does. You decide whether it is breaking molecules down, which is catabolism, or building them up, which is anabolism. Then you turn the card to check.

printables.title: 24 body cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: After lunch, your liver joins glucose units into glycogen.
items.b: Build up. Small units are joined into a bigger store. The liver pays for it with ATP.

items.f: At three in the night, your liver turns glycogen into glucose.
items.b: Break down. The store is cut back into glucose, which goes into the blood for the brain.

items.f: A muscle cell turns glucose into carbon dioxide and water while you run.
items.b: Break down. This is cellular respiration. It loads ATP and gives off heat.

items.f: New skin grows over a grazed knee.
items.b: Build up. Cells join amino acids into new proteins and make new cells.

items.f: Yeast turn sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide.
items.b: Break down. This is fermentation. The yeast get a little energy from each sugar molecule.

items.f: A hen's body makes the protein of an egg white from the grain she ate.
items.b: Build up. Amino acids from her food are joined into new protein.

items.f: A camel uses up the fat in their hump on a long walk.
items.b: Break down. The fat is broken down to carbon dioxide and water, for energy.

items.f: A baby's bones grow longer.
items.b: Build up. New bone material is added at the growing ends. Growth is anabolism.

items.f: In a sprouting moong seed, stored starch is cut into sugar.
items.b: Break down. The seedling breaks down the store to get sugar and energy.

items.f: A sprouting moong seed makes a new root.
items.b: Build up. The seedling joins small molecules into the walls and proteins of new cells.

items.f: A rice plant joins carbon dioxide and water into glucose in sunlight.
items.b: Build up. This is photosynthesis. The energy for the building comes from light.

items.f: An old red blood cell is taken apart in the spleen.
items.b: Break down. The cell lasted about four months. Its iron is saved and used again.

items.f: Your bone marrow makes about two million new red blood cells every second.
items.b: Build up. Building new cells needs amino acids, iron and a great deal of ATP.

items.f: Brown fat cells in a newborn baby break down fat to make heat.
items.b: Break down. Here the energy is not caught in ATP. Nearly all of it becomes heat.

items.f: A bar-headed goose lays down body fat before flying over the Himalayas.
items.b: Build up. Spare food is built into fat, a store for the journey.

items.f: A spider makes silk for a web.
items.b: Build up. Silk is a protein. The spider joins amino acids to make it.

items.f: A mushroom's threads take in sugar from a rotting leaf and use it for energy.
items.b: Break down. The fungus breaks the sugar down, as your cells do.

items.f: A cow's body makes milk fat and milk sugar for her calf.
items.b: Build up. Small molecules from her food are joined into the fat, sugar and protein of milk.

items.f: An arm kept in a plaster cast for six weeks gets thinner.
items.b: Break down. Muscle protein is always being broken down. In an unused muscle, less is rebuilt.

items.f: A weightlifter's muscle fibres get thicker over months of training.
items.b: Build up. Training makes muscle cells build more protein than they break down.

items.f: In your stomach, enzymes cut the protein of dal into shorter chains.
items.b: Break down. This is digestion, in the gut. It happens before metabolism in the cells, but it is breaking down too.

items.f: A cell copies all its DNA before it divides.
items.b: Build up. The cell joins millions of small units into two new strands, and spends ATP on each join.

items.f: A firefly uses up fuel to load the ATP that powers their light.
items.b: Break down. Breaking down fuel loads the ATP. Spending the ATP makes the light.

items.f: A Himalayan brown bear lives on body fat through the winter sleep.
items.b: Break down. The bear's cells break down stored fat for energy for months.

printables.title: 2 pile labels to cut out
items: BREAK DOWN (catabolism): large molecules are cut into smaller ones, and energy is released
BUILD UP (anabolism): small molecules are joined into larger ones, and energy is spent

rules: Put the two labels on the table, BREAK DOWN on the left and BUILD UP on the right. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, question side up.
The first player reads the top card aloud. On a count of three, every player points at one of the two labels.
Turn the card over and read the answer. Each player who pointed at the right label scores 1 point.
Put the card under the right label, and pass the pile to the next reader.
The game ends when the pile is used up. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: sort all 24 cards into two piles without looking at the backs. Then turn them over and count how many you got right. Play again another day and try to beat your score.

setup.art: Two paper labels on a table reading BREAK DOWN and BUILD UP, with a pile of cards between them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the two labels and the pile of cards.

setup.art: Three players pointing at the same time, two at one label and one at the other, while one of them holds up a card.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. On three, everyone points at a label.

setup.art: A card turned over to show its answer, being placed under the BUILD UP label.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card to check. Score a point if you were right.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 24 cards and the two labels. 2. Lay the labels on the table and shuffle the cards. 3. Read the two labels aloud together.
flow.say: Every card is something a living body does. We decide if it breaks molecules down or builds them up. The back of the card has the answer.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and labels. Lay out the labels. Shuffle the cards. Read the labels aloud.
flow.context: This is the first step of Break or Build? Here you set out the labels and the cards.

flow.do: 1. Play through the pile, following the rules. 2. After each card, the reader says in their own words why it is breaking down or building up. 3. Keep score on paper.
flow.say: Before you point, ask yourself one thing. Is the body cutting something big into small pieces, or joining small pieces into something big?
flow.kid: Read a card. Point at a label. Turn the card to check. Say why. Keep score.

ask.q: Which card was hardest to decide, and why?
good: The arm in a cast, because nothing seems to be happening.
The firefly, because loading ATP and spending ATP are both in one card.

flow.parent: Twelve cards are 'break down' and twelve are 'build up'. Children often put 'gets thinner' and 'uses up' under building, because they think of anything a body does as building. Let the card backs do the correcting.
flow.context: This step of Break or Build? is the game itself. You play through all 24 cards.

flow.do: 1. Lay all the cards out under their two labels. 2. Ask your child to find one break-down card that could supply the energy for one build-up card. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at both piles. Could a body do only the build-up cards and none of the break-down cards? Why, or why not?
flow.kid: Look at both piles. Could a body only build and never break down? Say why.

check.q: Could a body do only anabolism, building up, and no catabolism at all?
options: Yes, if the body ate enough food
Yes, but only while asleep
No, because building needs energy from breaking down
check.why: Every join costs ATP, and ATP is loaded by breaking molecules down. Choosing 'if it ate enough' forgets that food gives no energy until it is broken down. Plants are a special case: light loads their ATP by day, and they still break sugar down as well.

flow.context: This is the last step of Break or Build? Here you look at how the two piles depend on each other.

games.title: Budget Day: build the most body before the day ends
games.context: This is a dice game about how a body spends its energy through one day. Beans stand for energy. Each round you may get food, you must pay the cost of staying alive, and then you choose whether to build new body parts or to keep a store. You will see where most of the energy ends up.

printables.title: The body sheet: draw one for each player
items: Box 1, BLOOD: beans you have just eaten, ready to use
Box 2, STORE: glycogen and fat, kept for later
Box 3, BODY: beans you have built into new body parts
In the middle of the table, one katori for all players, labelled HEAT
A food pile of about 50 beans or large seeds for each player

printables.title: What the die means, and the score sheet
items: Roll 1 or 2: no food this round
Roll 3 or 4: a snack. Take 5 beans into BLOOD
Roll 5 or 6: a meal. Take 9 beans into BLOOD, then pay 1 of them to HEAT for digesting it
Staying alive: pay 3 beans to HEAT every round
Building: pay 3 beans. 2 go to BODY and 1 goes to HEAT
Final score: beans in BODY after 8 rounds: __
Beans in the HEAT katori at the end: __

rules: Each player draws a body sheet with three boxes: BLOOD, STORE and BODY. Each player starts with 4 beans in STORE. Put the HEAT katori and the food pile in the middle.
A game is 8 rounds. Each round stands for three hours of a day. In a round, every player does the next three things in order.
First, eat. Roll the die and take beans from the food pile, as the die table says.
Second, stay alive. Pay 3 beans into HEAT. Pay from BLOOD first, and then from STORE. If both are empty, pay from BODY. That means your body is breaking itself down for fuel.
Third, choose. To build, pay 3 beans from BLOOD or STORE: 2 go to BODY and 1 goes to HEAT. You may build as many times as you can pay for, or not at all.
At the end of your turn, move any beans left in BLOOD to STORE, because blood can carry only a little fuel.
After 8 rounds, the player with the most beans in BODY wins. If there is a tie, the bigger STORE wins.
Playing alone: play 8 rounds and write down your BODY score. Play again and try to beat it. Try one game where you build whenever you can, and one where you always keep 6 beans in STORE.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with three hand-drawn boxes labelled BLOOD, STORE and BODY, with four beans in the STORE box.
setup.caption: 1. Draw three boxes. Put 4 beans in STORE.

setup.art: A die beside a heap of beans and a small steel katori labelled HEAT in the middle of a table.
setup.caption: 2. Roll to eat. Then pay 3 beans to HEAT to stay alive.

setup.art: A child moving two beans into the BODY box and dropping one bean into the HEAT katori.
setup.caption: 3. Build if you can: 2 beans to BODY and 1 to HEAT.

flow.do: 1. Each player draws the three boxes. 2. Put 4 beans in each STORE box. 3. Put the HEAT katori and the food pile in the middle. 4. Read the die table and the rules aloud, and play one practice round.
flow.say: Each bean is a bit of energy from food. Your job is to build as much BODY as you can in one day without running out of fuel.
flow.kid: Draw three boxes. Put 4 beans in STORE. Read the rules. Play one practice round.
flow.parent: Any large seeds work: rajma, chana, groundnuts or tamarind seeds. A die from a ludo or snakes and ladders set is fine.
flow.context: This is the first step of Budget Day. Here you draw the body sheet and learn the rules.

flow.do: 1. Play rounds 1 to 4. 2. After round 4, each player counts their STORE and BODY. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Notice what you must pay before you are allowed to build anything. What happens when the die gives you no food?
flow.kid: Play four rounds. Eat, stay alive, then choose. Count your STORE and your BODY.

ask.q: What do you always have to pay for first?
good: Staying alive.
The 3 beans for staying alive come before any building.

ask.q: What is the STORE good for?
good: It pays for staying alive in a round with no food.
Without a store I would have to break down my BODY.

flow.context: This step of Budget Day is the first half of the day, rounds 1 to 4.

flow.do: 1. Play rounds 5 to 8. 2. Count each player's BODY beans and name the winner. 3. Tip out the HEAT katori and count the beans in it.
flow.say: The day is over. Count your BODY. Now let's count the HEAT katori. Where did most of the beans go?
flow.kid: Play four more rounds. Count your BODY beans. Then count the beans in HEAT.
flow.parent: With two players the HEAT katori usually ends with 50 to 60 beans, far more than both BODY boxes together.
flow.context: This step of Budget Day is the second half of the day and the final count.

flow.do: 1. Compare the HEAT count with the BODY and STORE counts. 2. Ask the questions below. 3. Read the card 'Why every step gives off heat'.
flow.say: Most of the beans ended in HEAT. Was that energy wasted? What did it do on the way there?
flow.kid: Compare HEAT with BODY and STORE. Where did most beans go? Was that energy wasted?

ask.q: Most beans ended as heat. What did they do before that?
good: They kept the body alive.
They paid for the heart, the brain and the other organs, and then left as heat.

ask.q: How is this game simpler than a real body?
good: A real body does not eat by rolling a die.
A real body uses energy every second, and uses more when it moves.

check.q: In Budget Day, a player with an empty BLOOD box and an empty STORE must pay from BODY. What does this copy?
options: A body that stops needing energy
A body turning heat back into food
A starving body breaks down its own muscle
check.why: The cost of staying alive must always be paid. When food and stores run out, the body breaks down its own protein for fuel. Choosing 'stops needing energy' is the mistake the game is built to show: a living body never stops needing energy.

flow.context: This is the last step of Budget Day. Here you look at where the energy ended up.

experiments.title: The Yeast Fuel Test: which foods can a yeast cell break down for energy?
experiments.context: In this experiment you give living yeast four different foods in four bottles. Yeast are tiny living beings, each one a single cell. When a yeast cell breaks food down for energy, they give off carbon dioxide gas. A balloon on each bottle catches the gas. You will find out which foods the yeast can use.
experiments.question: Which foods can yeast break down for energy: sugar, atta, a food you choose, or nothing at all? How can you tell from a balloon?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which bottle will have the biggest balloon after 30 minutes: no food, sugar, atta or your own food? Which will have no gas at all? Write your guesses and the reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the food. Every bottle is the same size and gets the same warm water, 100 millilitres, and the same yeast, one level teaspoon. Every food is two level teaspoons. Start all four bottles within two minutes of each other, and keep them side by side. Bottle A has yeast and no food. It shows what yeast do with nothing to eat.
results_table: My guess: big, small or none
Froth at 10 minutes: none, a little or a lot

materials.item: clean plastic bottles of the same size, 250 to 500 millilitres, such as small water bottles
balloons of the same size
dry yeast (instant or active dry), from a supermarket or a bakery shop
materials.qty: 4 level teaspoons, about one small packet

materials.item: sugar
atta (wheat flour)
one more food that you choose: powdered jaggery, honey, milk powder, salt, cooking oil or besan
warm water that feels just warm on the inside of your wrist, like a baby's bath
a teaspoon, a measuring cup or a marked tumbler, and a sheet of paper rolled into a funnel
a piece of string about 50 centimetres long, a ruler, a marker pen and a watch

experiments.safety: A grown-up mixes the warm water. Do not taste the mixtures, and pour them down the sink afterwards. Balloons can choke a small child, so keep them away from children under three.

schedule.what: Set up four bottles of yeast with four foods. Watch the froth, measure the balloons at 20 and 30 minutes, and explain the result.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for all four bottles. Draw a bar chart of the four balloons at 30 minutes. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: distance round each balloon after 30 minutes
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Four small plastic bottles in a row labelled A, B, C and D, with a spoon of yeast going into the first through a paper funnel.
setup.caption: 1. Label four bottles. Put one level teaspoon of yeast in each.

setup.art: The same four bottles with a different food beside each one: nothing, sugar, atta and a spoon of jaggery.
setup.caption: 2. Add no food to A, sugar to B, atta to C and your own food to D.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring warm water from a measuring cup into a bottle, with a child stretching a balloon over the neck of another bottle.
setup.caption: 3. Add 100 millilitres of warm water to each. Swirl, and fit a balloon.

setup.art: Four bottles after half an hour with balloons of different sizes, and a child measuring round the biggest balloon with a string.
setup.caption: 4. At 20 and 30 minutes, measure round each balloon with string.

flow.do: 1. Wash and label the four bottles A, B, C and D. 2. Blow up each balloon once and let the air out, so it stretches easily. 3. Put one level teaspoon of dry yeast into each bottle, using the paper funnel. 4. Let your child look at the yeast grains and smell them.
flow.say: These grains are dry yeast. Each grain holds a great many living cells, and they are resting. Water will wake them. What do you think they will need after that?
flow.kid: Label four bottles. Stretch four balloons. Put one teaspoon of yeast in each bottle. Look at the grains. Smell them.
flow.parent: Dry yeast keeps for months in a closed packet. If the packet is old or has been open for weeks, buy a new one. Any small bottles work if all four are the same.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Yeast Fuel Test. Here you get the bottles, the balloons and the yeast ready.

flow.do: 1. Put no food in bottle A. 2. Put two level teaspoons of sugar in B, and two of atta in C. 3. Your child chooses the food for D and adds two level teaspoons. 4. Ask for a guess and a reason for each bottle, and write them in the table.
flow.say: Bottle A gets yeast and no food. B gets sugar, C gets atta, and D is your choice. Which balloon will grow biggest? Which will stay flat? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Add no food to A. Add sugar to B and atta to C. Choose a food for D. Guess what each balloon will do. Say why.

ask.q: Why do we need bottle A, which has yeast and no food?
good: To see what yeast do without food.
So we know that any extra gas in the other bottles comes from the food.

flow.parent: Take any guess with a reason. Many children expect atta to do as well as sugar, because both are energy foods. Do not correct this now. The test will answer it.
flow.context: This step of the Yeast Fuel Test is where you add the foods and make your guesses.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up mixes hot and cold water until it feels just warm on the wrist. 2. Pour 100 millilitres into each bottle. 3. Hold a thumb over each top and swirl for ten seconds. 4. Stretch a balloon over each neck and note the time.
flow.say: The water must be warm, not hot. Hot water kills yeast. Let's fill all four quickly, so they start together.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up for warm water. Pour 100 ml into each bottle. Swirl each one. Fit the balloons. Note the time.
flow.parent: Water at about 35 to 40 degrees Celsius is right. It should feel pleasantly warm, never hot. If you have no measuring cup, use half a 200 millilitre tumbler for each bottle.
flow.context: This step of the Yeast Fuel Test starts the test. You add warm water and fit the balloons.

flow.do: 1. Stand the bottles side by side, away from a fan. 2. At 10 minutes, look for froth and bubbles and write what you see. 3. Let your child hold each bottle and smell near the neck. 4. While you wait, read the two cards on catabolism and anabolism together.
flow.say: Look closely at each bottle. Where do you see bubbles rising? Does any balloon stand up? What do you think the bubbles are?
flow.kid: Wait ten minutes. Look for froth and bubbles. Write what you see. Smell near each bottle.

ask.q: What do you notice, and what do you wonder?
good: The sugar bottle is frothing and its balloon is standing up.
I wonder why bottle A has no bubbles when the yeast are the same.

flow.parent: By 10 minutes the sugar bottle usually has a layer of froth and a balloon that stands upright. If it has no froth at all by 15 minutes, the yeast was old or the water too hot. Start again with new yeast.
flow.context: This step of the Yeast Fuel Test is the first look, ten minutes after the start.

flow.do: 1. At 20 minutes, wrap the string once round the widest part of each balloon. 2. Lay the string on the ruler and write the length. 3. Write 0 for a balloon that hangs limp. 4. Do the same at 30 minutes.
flow.say: We measure round the widest part of each balloon. A limp balloon scores zero. Let's measure all four now, and again in ten minutes.
flow.kid: At 20 minutes, measure round each balloon with string. Write it down. Do it again at 30 minutes.
flow.parent: The usual result: sugar gives a firm balloon, and jaggery or honey do nearly as well. Atta gives a small balloon or only a little froth. No food, salt and oil give almost nothing. Milk powder gives little, because yeast have no enzyme for milk sugar.
flow.context: This step of the Yeast Fuel Test is the measuring, at 20 and 30 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. 3. Only then, read the cards on catabolism and on respiration and fermentation.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: Which foods could the yeast break down? What is your evidence?
good: Sugar, because that balloon grew most.
Bottle A had the same yeast and water and made no gas, so the gas came from breaking down the food.

ask.q: Atta is an energy food for us. Why did the yeast make so little gas from it?
good: Atta is mostly starch, which is long chains of sugar units.
Yeast have no enzyme to cut starch, so they can use only the little sugar that is in the atta.

check.q: Bottle A had yeast and warm water but no food, and its balloon stayed flat. What does that show?
options: The yeast in bottle A were dead
Warm water alone makes the gas
The gas comes from yeast breaking down food
check.why: All four bottles had the same living yeast and the same warm water. Only the bottles with a food the yeast could break down made gas. Choosing 'warm water' forgets that bottle A had warm water too.

flow.think: Sugar might give off gas in warm water without any yeast. What fifth bottle would you add to check that?
flow.parent: A strong answer uses bottle A as evidence. The explanation: a yeast cell breaks sugar down to get energy, and carbon dioxide is what is left over. With little oxygen in the bottle, the yeast ferment the sugar, so alcohol is left over too. Your own cells break the same sugar down fully, with oxygen.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Yeast Fuel Test. You compare the four balloons and explain them.

experiments.title: The Lunch Test: what changes in your body after a meal?
experiments.context: In this two-day experiment you count your pulse and take your temperature before lunch, and twice after it. On the second day you do the same at the same times, but you eat only after the last measurement. You will find out whether a meal changes your pulse, your temperature or how warm you feel.
experiments.question: Does eating a meal change your pulse, your body temperature or how warm you feel? Or would those changes happen at that time of day anyway?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After lunch, will your pulse be faster, slower or the same? Will the thermometer read higher, lower or the same? Will you feel warmer? Write each guess and the reason for it.
experiments.fair_test: Change only one thing: whether you have eaten. Measure at the same three clock times on both days. Sit quietly for five minutes before each measurement, in the same chair and the same room. Do the same quiet thing in between, such as reading. Use the same thermometer in the same armpit. Count the pulse twice each time, because one count can be off.

materials.item: a digital fever thermometer
a watch or phone that shows seconds
a notebook and a pencil
your usual lunch

experiments.safety: On the second day lunch is about 75 minutes late. A child who feels unwell or very hungry should eat, and try the test another day.

schedule.what: Learn to count a pulse. Measure just before lunch, then 30 and 60 minutes after you finish eating.
Measure at the same three clock times without eating. Eat after the last measurement. Compare the two days.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for both days. Draw two lines on one graph, one for each day, showing your pulse at the three times. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A child sitting on a chair with two fingers of one hand on the inside of the other wrist, beside a clock that shows seconds.
setup.caption: 1. Sit for five minutes. Count your pulse for 30 seconds and double it.

setup.art: A child sitting still with a digital thermometer held under one arm.
setup.caption: 2. Take your temperature under the same arm each time.

setup.art: A notebook table with three rows for three clock times and a plate of lunch drawn between the first and second rows.
setup.caption: 3. Measure before lunch, and 30 and 60 minutes after it.

setup.art: The same notebook table for a second day, with the plate of lunch drawn after the last row.
setup.caption: 4. Next day, measure at the same times, and eat afterwards.

flow.do: 1. Show your child how to find the pulse at the wrist, below the thumb, with two fingers. 2. Count the beats for 30 seconds and double the number. 3. Practise twice. 4. Agree the warmth scores: 0 is cool, 1 is the same as usual, 2 is warm, 3 is hot.
flow.say: Press gently with two fingers, not your thumb. Count the beats for 30 seconds and double it. Let's practise until two counts nearly agree.
flow.kid: Find your pulse with two fingers. Count for 30 seconds. Double it. Practise twice. Learn the scores 0 to 3.
flow.parent: If the wrist pulse is hard to find, use the side of the neck beside the windpipe. Two counts within four beats of each other are good enough.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Lunch Test. Here you learn to count your pulse and agree the warmth scores.

flow.do: 1. Just before lunch, your child sits quietly for five minutes. 2. Count the pulse twice. 3. Take the temperature under the arm. 4. Write the warmth score, and ask for guesses about what will change after lunch, with reasons.
flow.say: These are your 'before' numbers. What do you think will change after lunch? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Sit quietly for five minutes. Count your pulse twice. Take your temperature. Write your warmth score. Guess what lunch will change.
flow.parent: Keep the arm pressed to the side until the thermometer beeps. Armpit readings are lower than mouth readings, and that is fine. Only the change matters here.
flow.context: This step of the Lunch Test is the measurement just before lunch on day 1.

flow.do: 1. Note the time when lunch ends. 2. Your child reads or draws quietly afterwards, without running about. 3. At 30 minutes, measure pulse, temperature and warmth as before. 4. At 60 minutes, measure all three again.
flow.say: No running after lunch today, because running would change your pulse too. We measure at 30 minutes and again at 60 minutes.
flow.kid: After lunch, sit and read. At 30 minutes, measure all three things. At 60 minutes, measure again.

ask.q: What changed, and what stayed the same?
good: My pulse went up by some beats.
My temperature hardly changed.
I felt warmer, mostly in my face and hands.

flow.parent: In many people the pulse is 5 to 15 beats a minute faster after a meal. The thermometer often changes by only one or two tenths of a degree, either way. That is about as small as the thermometer can show.
flow.context: This step of the Lunch Test is the two measurements after lunch on day 1.

flow.do: 1. On day 2, measure at the same three clock times as on day 1. 2. Your child sits and reads in between, as before, but does not eat. A drink of water is fine. 3. Serve lunch straight after the last measurement.
flow.say: Today we do everything the same, except that lunch comes after the last measurement. This shows us what your body does at these times without a meal.
flow.kid: Measure at the same three times as yesterday. Read in between. Do not eat yet. Eat after the last measurement.
flow.wait: Do this on the next day, starting at the same clock time.
flow.parent: If a late lunch is too hard, use a mid-morning hour on day 2 instead. Say clearly in the notebook that the time of day was different, because that makes the test less fair.
flow.context: This step of the Lunch Test is day 2. You measure at the same times without eating.

flow.do: 1. Put the two days side by side. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. 3. Only then, read the card 'Why you feel warm after eating'.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw on the two days, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Compare the two days. Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: Why did we need day 2?
good: To check that the change came from the meal and not from the time of day.
Pulse and temperature change a little through the day anyway.

ask.q: Your temperature hardly changed. Does that mean no extra heat was made?
good: No. The body can send extra heat out through the skin and keep its temperature steady.
That may be why my skin felt warmer.

check.q: After a meal the body makes extra heat, yet a thermometer shows almost no change. Why?
options: No extra heat is made after a meal
The body sends the extra heat out through the skin
The thermometer is broken
check.why: The brain keeps body temperature steady. When more heat is made, more blood goes to the skin and the heat leaves. Choosing 'no extra heat' mixes up heat with temperature: a body can make more heat and stay at the same temperature.

flow.think: One person on two days is a small test. How could you make the result more trustworthy?
flow.parent: A faster pulse on the lunch day and no change on the other day is good evidence that the meal caused it. If both days look the same, that is a real result too. Write it down as it is, and try again with a bigger meal.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Lunch Test. You compare the day with lunch and the day without.

activities.title: Warmer Than the Room: which stays warm, the water or you?
activities.context: In this activity you fill a tumbler with water that is as warm as your skin. You leave it on the table for half an hour and then feel the water and your own cheek. You will find out which of the two stays warm, and start to ask why.

materials.item: a steel tumbler
warm water, as warm as a comfortable bath
a digital fever thermometer, if you have one

activities.safety: A grown-up mixes the warm water. It should be comfortable to hold a finger in.
activities.record: Draw the tumbler and yourself at the start and after 30 minutes. Write 'warm' or 'cool' beside each. Under the drawing, write one sentence about what must be happening inside you.

setup.art: A child holding a steel tumbler of warm water in one hand with the other palm on a cheek.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the warm tumbler. Feel your cheek. Both are warm.

setup.art: The tumbler standing alone on a table beside a clock, while the child works at something else nearby.
setup.caption: 2. Leave the tumbler on the table for 30 minutes.

setup.art: The child with one finger in the tumbler and the other palm on a cheek, looking surprised.
setup.caption: 3. Feel the water and your cheek again. Which is still warm?

flow.do: 1. A grown-up fills the tumbler with comfortably warm water. 2. Your child dips a finger in the water, and puts the other palm on a cheek. 3. Ask what each will feel like in 30 minutes, and why. 4. Stand the tumbler on the table.
flow.say: The water and your cheek are both warm now. What will each feel like in half an hour? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Feel the warm water. Feel your cheek. Guess how each will feel in 30 minutes. Say why.
flow.parent: If you have a fever thermometer, take your child's temperature under the arm now. It will read about 36 to 37 degrees Celsius.
flow.context: This is the first step of Warmer Than the Room. Here you feel the warm water and your own cheek, and make a guess.

flow.do: 1. After about 30 minutes, your child dips a finger in the water again. 2. They put the other palm on a cheek. 3. If you have a thermometer, take their temperature again, and then put it in the water.
flow.say: Feel the water now, and feel your cheek. What has changed? What has not?
flow.kid: After 30 minutes, feel the water again. Feel your cheek again. What changed? What did not?
flow.wait: Do this about 30 minutes later. The Yeast Fuel Test fits well in between.
flow.parent: The water is now at room temperature and feels cool. A fever thermometer in it will usually show 'Lo', because it cannot read below 32 degrees. Your child's own temperature is the same as before.
flow.context: This step of Warmer Than the Room comes 30 minutes later. You compare the water and your cheek again.

flow.do: 1. Ask the two questions below and wait for your child's ideas. 2. Do not explain yet. 3. Write their best idea in the notebook, to check at the end of the unit.
flow.say: The water lost its heat to the room. You are in the same room. So why are you still warm?
flow.kid: The water lost its heat. You did not go cool. Why not? Say your best idea.

ask.q: You were losing heat to the room too. What must be happening inside you?
good: My body must be making new heat all the time.
Something in me keeps replacing the heat I lose.

ask.q: Where could that heat be coming from?
good: From food.
From my muscles or my blood.
I am not sure yet.

flow.think: Would the water have stayed warm if you had wrapped the tumbler in a shawl?
flow.parent: Take any idea. 'From food' is right, and this lesson explains how. A wrapped tumbler also cools, only more slowly. You can try it with a second tumbler.
