flow.context: This is the last step of Warmer Than the Room. Here you ask why the water went cool and you did not.

activities.title: The Wall Sit: feel a muscle use its fuel
activities.context: In this activity you sit against a wall with no chair and hold still for up to a minute. Your thigh muscles work hard without moving you anywhere. You will feel what happens in a muscle that is breaking down fuel fast.

materials.item: a clear wall and a floor that is not slippery
a watch that shows seconds

activities.safety: Do this in bare feet or shoes, not socks. Stop at once if a knee hurts. A child with a knee or leg injury should not do it.
activities.record: Write your pulse before and after. Write three things you felt in your thighs. Then write where you think the heat came from.

setup.art: A child standing with their back flat against a wall and feet a step away from it.
setup.caption: 1. Stand with your back on the wall and your feet one step out.

setup.art: The child slid down the wall until the thighs are level, as if sitting on an invisible chair, with a watch on the floor in front.
setup.caption: 2. Slide down until you are 'sitting'. Hold for up to one minute.

setup.art: The child standing again with a palm on one thigh and two fingers on the other wrist.
setup.caption: 3. Stand up. Feel your thighs and count your pulse.

flow.do: 1. Your child counts their pulse for 30 seconds and doubles it. 2. They lay a palm on one thigh and say how warm it feels. 3. Ask what they expect to feel in their thighs, and why.
flow.say: You are going to hold still, but your thigh muscles will be working hard. What do you think you will feel in them? Why?
flow.kid: Count your pulse. Feel how warm your thigh is. Guess what your thighs will feel. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Wall Sit. Here you take your pulse and make a guess.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands with their back against the wall and feet one step out. 2. They slide down until the thighs are level. 3. They hold still for up to 60 seconds, and say aloud what they feel. 4. They stand up when it is too hard.
flow.say: Slide down as if there were a chair. Hold still, and tell me what your thighs feel like as the seconds pass.
flow.kid: Slide down the wall. Hold still like sitting on a chair. Say what your thighs feel. Stand up when it is too hard.
flow.parent: Most children of nine or ten hold for 30 to 60 seconds. They usually report a burning feeling, then shaking. Neither is harmful, and both stop within a minute of standing up.
flow.context: This step of the Wall Sit is the sit itself. You hold still for up to a minute.

flow.do: 1. Straight away, your child lays a palm on a thigh again. 2. They count their pulse for 30 seconds and double it. 3. They notice their breathing. 4. Ask the questions below, and then read the card on energy stores.
flow.say: Feel your thigh and count your pulse now. You did not go anywhere. So where did all that energy go?
flow.kid: Feel your thigh. Count your pulse. Notice your breathing. Where did the energy go?

ask.q: You did not move. Why was that so tiring?
good: My muscles had to keep pulling to hold me up.
They were spending energy the whole time, even though nothing moved.

ask.q: Why did your pulse and breathing speed up?
good: The muscles needed more oxygen and fuel.
The blood had to carry away more carbon dioxide and heat.

check.q: In a wall sit nothing moves, yet the thigh muscles get warm. Where does the heat come from?
options: The wall rubbing on your back
Hot blood sent from the heart
Muscle cells breaking fuel down fast
check.why: A muscle holding still is still spending ATP, and its cells break down glucose and glycogen to reload it. Heat escapes at every step. Choosing 'hot blood' has it backwards: the muscle warms the blood.

flow.parent: The burning feeling comes from muscle cells breaking glucose down faster than oxygen can arrive. They make lactate, which the blood carries away within the hour. Lactate does not cause next-day soreness.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Wall Sit. You feel your thighs, count your pulse and explain what happened.

activities.title: Twenty Beans: where does a resting body spend its energy?
activities.context: In this activity 20 beans stand for all the energy a resting adult uses. You place the beans on a drawing of a body to show which parts you think use the most. Then you compare your guess with real measurements.

materials.item: rajma, chana or any large seeds
a large sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.record: Draw the body with its seven boxes. In each box write your guess and the measured number of beans. Circle the box that surprised you most.

setup.art: A simple outline of a human body on paper with seven labelled boxes: brain, liver, heart, kidneys, muscles, fat, and everything else.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a body with seven boxes.

setup.art: A child placing beans from a small heap of twenty into the boxes on the drawing.
setup.caption: 2. Share out 20 beans to show your guess.

setup.art: The same drawing with the measured numbers written beside each box and the beans moved to match.
setup.caption: 3. Move the beans to the measured numbers. What surprised you?

flow.do: 1. Draw the outline of a body on the paper. 2. Draw seven boxes and label them: brain, liver, heart, kidneys, muscles, fat, everything else. 3. Explain that 'everything else' means skin, gut, lungs, bones and blood. 4. Count out 20 beans.
flow.say: These 20 beans are all the energy a grown-up uses while lying still. Each bean is one twentieth of it.
flow.kid: Draw a body. Draw seven boxes. Label them. Count out 20 beans.
flow.context: This is the first step of Twenty Beans. Here you draw a body with seven boxes and count out the beans.

flow.do: 1. Your child shares out the 20 beans among the boxes. 2. They say why they gave the most beans to that box. 3. Write the guess beside each box.
flow.say: The person is lying still. Which parts are using the energy? Share out the beans, and tell me why you chose that way.
flow.kid: Share the 20 beans among the boxes. Which part uses most? Say why.
flow.parent: Most children give the muscles or the heart the most. Few think of the liver or the kidneys. Take any guess with a reason.
flow.context: This step of Twenty Beans is your guess. You share out the beans among the parts of the body.

flow.do: 1. Read out the measured numbers: brain 4, liver 4, muscles 4, heart 2, kidneys 2, fat 1, everything else 3. 2. Your child moves the beans to match. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Here are the measured numbers. Move the beans to match them. Which box surprised you most?
flow.kid: Move the beans. Brain 4, liver 4, muscles 4. Heart 2, kidneys 2, fat 1. Everything else 3. What surprised you?

ask.q: The brain, liver, heart and kidneys together are about one twentieth of the body's weight. How many of the 20 beans do they use?
good: 12 of the 20 beans, which is more than half.

ask.q: Muscles are about 40 parts in 100 of the body's weight. Why do they get only 4 beans?
good: Because the person is resting.
A resting muscle uses little energy for its size.

flow.parent: The numbers are for a man of 70 kilograms, rounded to whole beans. They come from measurements of how much energy each organ uses, collected by Marinos Elia in 1992.
flow.context: This step of Twenty Beans compares your guess with the measurements.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that a body of about five years old is different. 2. Move beans until 13 of the 20 are on the brain. 3. Ask what that might mean for a young child's growth.
flow.say: At about five years old, the brain uses about two thirds of the resting energy. That is 13 beans. What is left for growing?
flow.kid: Now put 13 beans on the brain. That is a five-year-old. How many are left for the rest?

check.q: Children put on weight most slowly at about four to five years old. What does the bean count suggest?
options: Children eat nothing at that age
Muscles use most of the energy then
The brain is using much of the energy then
check.why: A study in 2014 found that body growth is slowest at the ages when the brain uses the most glucose. Energy spent in one place cannot be spent in another. Choosing 'muscles' forgets that resting muscle uses little.

flow.parent: The study is by Christopher Kuzawa and colleagues. It shows that the two things happen at the same ages. It does not prove that one causes the other.
flow.context: This is the last step of Twenty Beans. Here you see how much of a young child's energy goes to the brain.

activities.title: One Idli's Journey: draw where the atoms and the energy go
activities.context: In this activity you draw a map of what happens to one idli and a spoon of sambar after they are digested. You follow the glucose and the amino acids along every road they can take inside your cells. You mark which roads break molecules down, which build them up, and where heat escapes.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper
a pencil and three colour pencils: red, blue and orange

activities.record: Keep the finished map. Under it, write one sentence that answers this: where is this morning's idli now?

setup.art: A sheet of paper with an idli drawn at the top and three empty roads leading down from it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw an idli at the top. Guess where it will be tomorrow.

setup.art: The same map with three roads labelled: broken down now, stored as glycogen, stored as fat, and a fourth road for amino acids being built into muscle.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the roads the glucose and the amino acids can take.

setup.art: The finished map with red roads for breaking down, blue roads for building up, and small orange wavy lines for heat on every road.
setup.caption: 3. Colour breaking down red, building up blue, and heat orange.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws an idli and a spoon of sambar at the top of the paper. 2. Ask where this food will be at this time tomorrow, and why they think so. 3. Write the guess at the side.
flow.say: You eat this idli at eight in the morning. Where will it be at eight tomorrow morning? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw an idli and some sambar. Where will they be tomorrow? Say why you think so.
flow.parent: Common answers are 'in the toilet' and 'in my tummy'. Only the fibre and a little else leaves in the toilet. Most of the meal crosses into the blood.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Idli's Journey. Here you guess where a meal ends up.

flow.do: 1. Draw an arrow from the idli to the word 'glucose', and from the sambar dal to 'amino acids'. 2. From glucose, draw three roads. Road 1: broken down now, to carbon dioxide and water. Road 2: joined into glycogen in the liver and muscles. Road 3: stored as fat, if the stores are full. 3. From amino acids, draw two roads. Road 4: joined into your own proteins. Road 5: broken down, with the nitrogen leaving as urea in urine. 4. At the end of roads 1 and 5, draw lungs breathing out carbon dioxide.
flow.say: Inside your cells the glucose can take three roads, and the amino acids two. Let's draw all five and say what happens on each.
flow.kid: Draw glucose and amino acids. Draw three roads from glucose. Draw two roads from amino acids. Add lungs breathing out.
flow.parent: Most of the glucose from one idli takes road 1 or road 2 within hours. Glycogen made on road 2 is broken down again that night and joins road 1. Road 3 is mostly for fat from the meal itself, though the liver can also build fat from spare glucose.
flow.context: This step of One Idli's Journey is the map itself. You draw the five roads food molecules can take in your cells.

flow.do: 1. Your child colours the breaking-down roads red, which are roads 1 and 5. 2. They colour the building-up roads blue, which are roads 2, 3 and 4. 3. They draw a small orange wavy line for heat on every road. 4. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Red is for catabolism, breaking down. Blue is for anabolism, building up. Now mark with orange every road where heat escapes.
flow.kid: Colour breaking-down roads red. Colour building-up roads blue. Draw orange heat lines where heat escapes.

ask.q: On which roads does heat escape?
good: On all of them.
Breaking down gives off heat, and building up spends ATP, which gives off heat too.

ask.q: So where is the idli at eight tomorrow morning?
good: Most of its carbon has been breathed out as carbon dioxide.
Some may still be in me as glycogen, fat or protein.

check.q: Your liver joins glucose units into glycogen after a meal. What is this?
options: Catabolism, and it releases energy
Digestion in the gut
Anabolism, and it costs energy
check.why: Joining small units into a bigger molecule is anabolism, and the cell pays for it with ATP. Choosing 'digestion' mixes up the gut with the cells: digestion cuts food up before it enters the blood.

flow.context: This is the last step of One Idli's Journey. You colour the roads and mark where heat escapes.

projects.title: Grown in the Dark: what does a seedling build with, when there is no light?
projects.context: In this five-day project you sprout moong seeds in a closed, dark place, with only water. A plant cannot make food without light. You watch each seedling build a root and a long shoot anyway, and you watch what happens to the two thick seed leaves. You will find out where the material and the energy for the new parts come from.

materials.item: whole green moong (green gram)
a steel dabba with a lid, or a bowl with a plate to cover it
a clean cotton cloth or a thick layer of cotton wool
water
a ruler and a notebook

projects.safety: Rinse the seedlings with fresh water each day. If they smell sour or grow fluffy mould, throw them away and start again. Do not eat seedlings from this project.

schedule.what: In the evening, soak 20 moong seeds in water. Keep 5 dry seeds aside to compare.
Drain the seeds. Split one open and draw it. Lay the rest on a wet cloth in the dabba, close it and put it in a cupboard.
Rinse, and measure the three longest seedlings. Look at the seed leaves.
Rinse, measure the three longest seedlings and look at the seed leaves again.
Measure for the last time. Compare the seed leaves with a freshly soaked seed, and explain where the new parts came from.

projects.record: Make a table with a row for each day: the length of the three longest seedlings, their mean, and one line about how the seed leaves look. On day 5, draw a soaked seed and a five-day seedling side by side. Then write where you think the root and shoot came from.

setup.art: Twenty green moong seeds soaking in a small steel bowl of water, with five dry seeds on a saucer beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Soak 20 moong seeds overnight. Keep 5 dry.

setup.art: Soaked seeds spread on a wet cloth inside a steel dabba, with the lid about to go on and an open cupboard behind.
setup.caption: 2. Lay the seeds on a wet cloth in a dabba. Close it and keep it in the dark.

setup.art: A child measuring a long, pale, thin seedling against a ruler, with two small yellow wrinkled seed leaves near the top.
setup.caption: 3. Each day, measure the longest seedlings and look at the seed leaves.

flow.do: 1. In the evening, put 20 moong seeds in a bowl and cover them with water. 2. Put 5 dry seeds on a saucer beside the bowl. 3. Ask your child what a seed will need in order to grow a root and a shoot.
flow.say: These seeds will get water and air, and no light at all. What will they need, to build a root and a shoot? Where could they get it?
flow.kid: Soak 20 moong seeds in water. Keep 5 dry. What will a seed need to grow? Say your idea.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Grown in the Dark. Here you soak the seeds and say what you think they will need.

flow.do: 1. Next morning, drain the seeds and compare them with the dry ones. 2. Split one soaked seed with a fingernail and draw the two thick halves and the tiny plant between them. 3. Wet the cloth, wring it out and lay it in the dabba. 4. Spread the seeds on it, close the lid and put the dabba in a cupboard. 5. Ask for a guess: will the seedlings grow in the dark, and what will happen to the thick halves? Why?
flow.say: The two thick halves are the seed leaves. Will a seedling grow in the dark? What will happen to the seed leaves? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Split one soaked seed. Draw the two halves. Lay the others on a wet cloth. Close the dabba. Guess what will happen.
flow.wait: Do this the next morning, after the seeds have soaked for 8 to 12 hours.
flow.parent: The seed leaves are also called cotyledons. They are packed with starch and protein that the parent plant stored for the young one. The lid need not be airtight. The seeds need air.
flow.context: This is day 2 of Grown in the Dark. Here you look inside a seed and put the rest in the dark.

flow.do: 1. Each day for two days, rinse the seedlings gently and drain them. 2. Measure the three longest seedlings from root tip to shoot tip, and find the mean. 3. Look at the seed leaves and write one line about them. 4. Close the dabba and put it back.
flow.say: Measure the three longest, and tell me how the seed leaves look today. Are they as fat as before?
flow.kid: Rinse the seedlings. Measure the three longest. Find the mean. Look at the seed leaves. Put them back in the dark.
flow.wait: Do this once a day on the next two days.
flow.parent: In warm weather the seedlings reach 5 to 10 centimetres by day 5. They are pale and thin, because they have had no light. In cool weather they grow more slowly, so allow two more days.
flow.context: These are days 3 and 4 of Grown in the Dark. Each day you measure the seedlings and look at the seed leaves.

flow.do: 1. On day 5, measure for the last time. 2. Soak a dry seed for an hour and split the seed open. Lay the two halves beside the seed leaves of a seedling. 3. Your child draws both, and says what has changed. 4. Ask the questions below. 5. Only then, read the card on anabolism.
flow.say: The seedling had water, air and darkness. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and where you think the new root and shoot came from.
flow.kid: Measure one last time. Compare old and new seed leaves. Draw both. Say where the new parts came from.

ask.q: What happened to the seed leaves as the shoot grew?
good: They got thinner, wrinkled and yellow.
They shrank while the root and shoot got bigger.

ask.q: The seedling got no food from outside and no light. Where did the material and the energy come from?
good: From the food stored in the seed leaves.
The seedling broke down the store. They used some for energy and built the rest into new parts.

check.q: A moong seedling grows 8 centimetres in the dark. Scientists dry and weigh such seedlings. What do they find?
options: The dry seedling weighs much more than the dry seed
The dry seedling weighs less than the dry seed
The weight is exactly the same
check.why: The seedling is bigger, but most of the extra size is water. Part of the stored food was broken down for energy, and its carbon left as carbon dioxide. Choosing 'much more' is natural, but without light the seedling has taken in no new food.

flow.parent: This is catabolism and anabolism in one small body. The seedling breaks down the stored starch and protein. Some of it is used for energy, and some is rebuilt into roots and stems. You can plant the seedlings in a pot afterwards, and they will turn green in the light.
flow.context: This is day 5 of Grown in the Dark. Here you compare the seed leaves and explain how the seedling grew.

challenges.title: Hold It at 37: keep a tumbler as warm as a body, with the least fuel
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. In Warmer Than the Room, a tumbler of warm water went cool because nothing inside it made heat. Here the tumbler stands in cold water, and you keep it near 37 degrees Celsius by adding teaspoons of hot water. Each spoon stands for food. Then you redesign the set-up so that it needs fewer spoons.
challenges.problem: A steel tumbler of warm water stands in a vessel of tap water. Keep the water in the tumbler between 36 and 38 degrees Celsius for 10 minutes. Use as few teaspoons of hot water as you can.
constraints: The tumbler must stay standing in the vessel of tap water for the whole 10 minutes.
The only heat you may add is hot water, one teaspoon at a time.
Measure the temperature every 2 minutes, and add a spoon only when it reads below 36.5 degrees.
materials: a steel tumbler with 150 millilitres of warm water
a wide vessel with tap water 5 centimetres deep
a flask or mug of hot water and a teaspoon
a digital fever thermometer or a kitchen thermometer
things to redesign with: a bigger empty vessel, a steel plate for a lid, a plastic bag, a dry sock, a second tumbler
general: Cover the tumbler with a steel plate, so that less heat leaves from the top.
Stand the tumbler inside a bigger empty vessel that floats or stands in the tap water. The layer of air between them slows the heat.
Put a dry sock on the tumbler and a plastic bag over the sock, to keep the sock dry.
creative: Use a bigger tumbler with twice the water. A big body has less surface for its size, so it loses heat more slowly. That is one reason an elephant needs less food for each kilogram than a shrew.
Stand three warm tumblers touching each other in the vessel. Each one shields the others. Honey bees keep warm in winter by packing together in the same way.
A duck's feathers are oiled, so the fluffy layer under them stays dry and full of air. Copy this with a dry cotton layer inside a waterproof one.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own way to hold 37 degrees with the fewest spoons. Test it for 10 minutes. How many spoons did it need? Which animal keeps warm in the way your design does?

setup.art: A steel tumbler of water standing in a wide vessel of tap water, with a thermometer in the tumbler and a mug of hot water and a teaspoon beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Stand the warm tumbler in tap water. Add hot water by the teaspoon to hold 37 degrees.

setup.art: The same tumbler now sitting inside a larger empty vessel that stands in the tap water, with a steel plate as a lid.
setup.caption: 2. Redesign it to lose less heat, and count the spoons again.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up fills the tumbler with 150 millilitres of water at about 38 degrees. 2. Stand the tumbler in the vessel of tap water. 3. Every 2 minutes, take the temperature of the water in the tumbler. 4. When it reads below 36.5 degrees, a grown-up adds one teaspoon of hot water and stirs. 5. After 10 minutes, write the number of spoons.
flow.say: First we need the number to beat. The tap water takes heat away, and each spoon of hot water puts some back. Let's count the spoons for 10 minutes.
flow.kid: Stand the warm tumbler in tap water. Check the temperature every 2 minutes. Ask a grown-up to add hot water. Count the spoons.
flow.parent: A fever thermometer takes up to a minute for each reading, and must be switched off and on between readings. Expect to add a spoon at almost every reading. In a real body the heat is made inside, by the cells. Here it comes from outside, but the counting works the same way.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hold It at 37. Here you count how many spoons of hot water a bare tumbler needs.

flow.do: 1. Look at the usual ideas: a lid, an air gap, a dry sock in a bag. 2. Your child chooses one and says why it should save spoons. 3. Start again with fresh warm water and count the spoons for 10 minutes.
flow.say: Which idea do you think will save the most spoons? Why? Let's test your choice for 10 minutes.
flow.kid: Pick one idea. Say why it should work. Test it for 10 minutes. Count the spoons.

ask.q: The tumbler needed fewer spoons this time. Did it make more heat, or lose less?
good: It lost less heat.
The spoons are the only heat going in, so fewer spoons means less heat was leaving.

flow.context: This step of Hold It at 37 tests one of the usual ideas.

flow.do: 1. Your child plans their own design and says what each part is for. 2. They build it and test it for 10 minutes. 3. They compare the number of spoons with the first two tests.
flow.say: Now design your own. What will you change, and why? How many spoons did it need?
flow.kid: Plan your own design. Build it. Test it for 10 minutes. Count the spoons.

check.q: A sparrow fluffs up their feathers on a cold morning. How does this save food?
options: Less heat leaves, so less fuel is needed
The feathers make extra heat
Fluffing stops the sparrow feeling hungry
check.why: Fluffed feathers hold a thicker layer of still air, which slows the heat leaving the body. The body then needs to break down less fuel to stay warm. Choosing 'the feathers make heat' is the blanket mistake: feathers make no heat.

flow.context: This is the last step of Hold It at 37. Here you build and test your own design.

challenges.title: The Balloon Race: get the most gas from one teaspoon of sugar
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. In the Yeast Fuel Test, yeast broke sugar down and filled a balloon with carbon dioxide. Here every bottle gets the same yeast, the same sugar and the same water. You change only the conditions around the yeast, to make them work as fast as they can.
challenges.problem: Each bottle gets one level teaspoon of yeast, one level teaspoon of sugar and 100 millilitres of water. Make the balloon as big as you can in 20 minutes by changing only the conditions.
constraints: The amounts of yeast, sugar and water are the same in every bottle.
You may change the warmth of the water, what stands around the bottle, and how you mix it.
Measure round every balloon with string at exactly 20 minutes.
materials: 2 or 3 small plastic bottles of the same size
dry yeast, sugar and a teaspoon
tap water, warm water and a vessel to make a warm bath
a towel, string, a ruler and a watch
general: Use water that feels just warm on the wrist, in place of cool tap water.
Stand the bottle in a vessel of warm water, so it stays warm for the whole 20 minutes.
Wrap the bottle in a towel to keep its warmth in.
creative: Wake the yeast first. Stir them into the warm water with a pinch of the sugar, wait five minutes, and then add the rest. Bakers do this.
Swirl the bottle gently every five minutes, so that every yeast cell meets fresh sugar.
Test water that is hot to the touch in one bottle. Find out what too much heat does to living cells.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own best conditions for yeast. Test them against a bottle made with cool tap water. How much bigger was your balloon? What does that tell you about why your own body stays at 37 degrees?

setup.art: Two small bottles with balloons, one standing on a table and one standing in a vessel of warm water wrapped in a towel.
setup.caption: 1. Give every bottle the same yeast, sugar and water. Change only the conditions.

setup.art: A child measuring round two balloons of different sizes with a piece of string, beside a watch showing 20 minutes.
setup.caption: 2. At 20 minutes, measure round each balloon.

flow.do: 1. Make one bottle with cool tap water: one teaspoon of yeast, one of sugar, and 100 millilitres of water. 2. Fit a balloon and note the time. 3. At 20 minutes, measure round the balloon and write it down as the size to beat.
flow.say: First we need the size to beat. This bottle gets cool tap water and nothing else to help it.
flow.kid: Make one bottle with cool tap water. Fit a balloon. At 20 minutes, measure it. Write it down.
flow.parent: To save time, start this bottle and the bottle in step 2 together.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Balloon Race. Here you find the balloon size for cool tap water.

flow.do: 1. Look at the usual ideas: warm water, a warm bath, a towel. 2. Your child chooses one and says why it should help the yeast. 3. Make the bottle, and measure the balloon at 20 minutes.
flow.say: Which idea do you think will help the yeast most? Why? Let's test your choice.
flow.kid: Pick one idea. Say why it should work. Make the bottle. Measure the balloon at 20 minutes.

ask.q: Why does a warm bottle make gas faster than a cool one?
good: The chemical changes in the yeast cells go faster when it is warm.
The enzymes work faster in warmth.

flow.context: This step of the Balloon Race tests one of the usual ideas.

flow.do: 1. Your child plans their own conditions and says what each change is for. 2. They make the bottle and measure the balloon at 20 minutes. 3. They compare it with the first two balloons.
flow.say: Now design your own best conditions. What will you change, and why? Did your balloon beat the others?
flow.kid: Plan your own conditions. Make the bottle. Measure at 20 minutes. Did you beat the others?
flow.parent: Yeast work fastest at about 30 to 38 degrees Celsius. Above about 50 degrees they begin to die, and the balloon stays flat. A flat balloon in the hot bottle is a useful result.

check.q: A bottle made with very hot water gave no gas at all. Why?
options: The heat killed the yeast cells
Hot water has no room for gas
The sugar was used up at once
check.why: The enzymes in a cell are proteins, and too much heat spoils their shape for good. The cell's metabolism then stops. Choosing 'the sugar was used up' forgets that using sugar up would have made gas.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Balloon Race. Here you test your own design.

worksheets.title: Metabolism: breaking down, building up and heat (core)

items.p: What is metabolism?
opts: The squeezing of food along the gut
All the chemical changes inside living cells
The speed at which you eat
items.why: Metabolism is every chemical change in a cell, both breaking down and building up. Choosing 'the gut' mixes it up with digestion, which happens before the food enters the cells.

items.p: Sort these into catabolism (breaking down) and anabolism (building up).
items: glucose is turned into carbon dioxide and water
amino acids are joined into muscle protein
glucose units are joined into glycogen
body fat is used on a long walk
items.why: Cutting glycogen, fat or glucose into smaller pieces is catabolism. Joining small units into glycogen, protein or bone is anabolism.

items.p: Building molecules up costs energy. The small molecule that carries this energy inside a cell is called ____.
items.why: ATP is loaded with energy when food is broken down, and spent wherever the cell needs energy. 'Glucose' is the fuel, not the carrier.

items.p: True or false: your body stops using energy when you lie completely still.
items.why: False. The heart, brain, liver and kidneys work all the time. The energy a resting body uses is its basal metabolic rate.

items.p: A tumbler of warm water goes cool in an hour, and you do not. Why?
opts: Your skin stops all heat leaving
Your cells keep making heat from food
The room heats you but not the water
items.why: You lose heat to the room all the time, just as the water does. Your cells replace it by breaking down food. Choosing 'skin stops heat' is the blanket mistake: skin only slows the heat.

items.p: In the Yeast Fuel Test, why did every bottle get the same yeast and the same water?
items.a: So that the food was the only thing that changed. Then any difference between the balloons must come from the food.
items.why: A strong answer says that a fair test changes one thing only, and names that thing: the food.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: Catabolism
breaking large molecules into smaller ones
Anabolism
joining small molecules into larger ones
Glycogen
a store of glucose in the liver and muscles
Metabolic rate
how fast a body uses energy
Fermentation
getting energy from sugar without oxygen
items.why: These words are used all through the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each.

items.p: Which gas filled the balloons in the Yeast Fuel Test?
items.why: Yeast give off carbon dioxide when they break sugar down. Choosing 'oxygen' mixes yeast up with a plant in sunlight, which gives off oxygen.

items.p: Put these in order, from a meal to the heat of your skin.
items: The cell spends the ATP on its work
The energy leaves the body as heat
Starch in rice is cut into glucose in the gut
A cell breaks glucose down and loads ATP
a: Starch in rice is cut into glucose in the gut
A cell breaks glucose down and loads ATP
The cell spends the ATP on its work
The energy leaves the body as heat
items.why: Digestion comes first, then the blood carries glucose to the cells. The cells break it down, spend the ATP, and the energy ends as heat.

items.p: True or false: a blanket makes heat.
items.why: False. A blanket only slows the heat leaving a body. The heat is made by the body's cells as they break down food.

items.p: Where does the body keep its large, long-lasting store of energy?
items.why: Fat holds the most energy for each gram. Glycogen in the liver and muscles is a smaller, quicker store. The blood carries only a little fuel at any moment.

items.p: Draw a yeast cell with sugar going in. Show two things that come out, and label them.
items.art: A blank oval for a yeast cell with one arrow pointing in and two empty arrows pointing out.
items.a: A cell with an arrow of sugar going in, and arrows of carbon dioxide and alcohol coming out. A heat arrow or an ATP label is a bonus.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the sugar is changed into something else. A drawing where the sugar simply vanishes misses that atoms are never lost.

items.p: After a meal the body uses extra energy to digest and store the food. This is called the ____ effect of food.
items.why: The thermic effect of food is the extra energy used to handle a meal. It ends as heat, which is one reason you feel warmer after eating.

items.p: A grown-up no longer grows. Give one reason their body still needs to build new molecules every day.
items.a: The body breaks down and rebuilds its own proteins and cells all the time. Red blood cells, skin and the gut lining wear out and are replaced.
items.why: A strong answer names turnover, or gives an example such as skin, blood cells or a healing cut.

items.p: Three people talk about the heat a body gives off.

views.says: The heat is waste. A perfect body would turn all its food into useful work.
The heat is useful. A lamb or a kid that cannot make enough of it dies of cold.
The heat is neither. It is what you get whenever a cell passes energy on.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Give one fact from the unit as evidence. Then say what one of the others has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses facts from the unit, such as heat escaping at every step, or mammals and birds needing it to stay warm. It chooses one view and gives a fair point from another.
items.why: All three have part of it. The heat cannot be avoided, mammals and birds depend on it, and it shows that the cells are at work.

worksheets.title: Stores, budgets and where the atoms go (stretch)

items.p: After a meal, where do most of the atoms of the fuel your cells burned end up?
opts: In the air, as carbon dioxide you breathed out
items.why: The carbon atoms leave as carbon dioxide in your breath, and the hydrogen atoms leave in water. Choosing 'turn into energy' is a common mistake: atoms are not turned into energy in a body.

items.p: True or false: lactate from a hard sprint is a waste that the body throws away.
items.why: False. Lactate is a fuel. The heart burns it, and the liver builds it back into glucose. Gerty Cori and Carl Cori described this cycle in 1929.

items.p: In Twenty Beans, the brain, liver, heart and kidneys use 4, 4, 2 and 2 beans. How many is that altogether?
items.why: 4 + 4 + 2 + 2 = 12. So these four organs use 12 of the 20 beans, which is more than half.

items.p: Why does the liver break down glycogen at night?
opts: To keep glucose in the blood while you are not eating
items.why: Your brain needs glucose all night, and you are not eating. The liver lets glucose out of its glycogen store to keep the blood level steady.

items.p: Put these stores in the order a fasting body uses them, from first to last.
items.why: Blood glucose lasts minutes, and liver glycogen about a day. Then fat becomes the main fuel. The body breaks down much muscle protein only when little fat is left.

items.p: In Grown in the Dark, the seed leaves shrank while the shoot grew. Explain why, using 'break down' and 'build up'.
items.a: The seedling broke down the starch and protein stored in the seed leaves. Some gave energy, and some of the pieces were built up into the new root and shoot.
items.why: A strong answer links the two: the building was paid for, and supplied, by the breaking down.

items.p: Which meal costs the body the most energy to digest and store, for the same energy eaten?
items.why: Protein costs the most to handle, carbohydrate less, and fat the least. Choosing 'the same' is reasonable if you have not met the thermic effect of food.

items.p: A cell that breaks glucose down without oxygen gets much ____ energy than a cell that uses oxygen.
items.why: Without oxygen the glucose is broken only part of the way, so most of its energy stays in the alcohol or lactate that is left.

items.p: On a drawing of a body, label two places that store glycogen and one that stores fat.
items.art: An outline of a human body showing the liver, the leg and arm muscles and the layer under the skin, with three blank label lines.
items.why: Fat around the organs in the belly is also right for the fat store.

items.p: True or false: for each kilogram of body, a shrew uses energy faster than an elephant.
items.why: True. A small warm body loses heat quickly, so each gram of it must make more heat. An Etruscan shrew eats up to twice their own weight a day.

items.p: In the Lunch Test, why must you measure at the same clock times on a day without lunch?
items.a: Pulse and temperature change a little through the day anyway. The second day shows those changes, so the rest must be due to the meal.
items.why: A strong answer says the second day is there for comparison, and that it rules out the time of day as the cause.

items.p: Match each living being to the way they manage their energy.
pairs: Honey bees in winter
pack together and shiver their flight muscles
A python
eats one huge meal and then rests for weeks
A Himalayan brown bear
lives on body fat through a winter sleep
A sacred lotus flower
breaks down stored food fast and warms itself
A newborn baby
makes heat in brown fat without shivering
items.why: Each of these beings solves the same problem, staying alive on the fuel they have, in a different way.

items.p: A person's body uses up 10 kilograms of stored fat. About how much of it leaves through the lungs?
items.why: About 8.4 kilograms leave as carbon dioxide, and the other 1.6 kilograms leave as water. The carbon atoms of the fat are breathed out.

items.p: Draw one glucose molecule entering a muscle cell. Show where its energy goes, using three arrows.
items.art: A blank muscle cell with one glucose molecule at its edge.
items.a: Arrows to ATP, to heat, and from the ATP to the muscle's work. The best drawings show the heat arrow thicker than the ATP arrow.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that only part of the energy is caught in ATP, and that the rest leaves as heat at once.

items.p: Two people explain why a child's body puts on weight most slowly at about five years old.

views.says: At that age the brain uses so much energy that less is left for growing.
The two things happen at the same age. That does not prove one causes the other.

items.ask: Which view do you find stronger? Say what evidence would help to settle it.
items.a: A strong answer uses the finding that the brain uses the most energy at about that age. It also notes that two things happening together does not prove that one causes the other.
items.why: The first view fits the measurements. The second is a fair warning about what those measurements can prove.

items.p: A flame and a cell both break fuel down with oxygen. Give two things a cell does that a flame does not.
items.a: A cell breaks the fuel down in many small steps and catches part of the energy in ATP. A cell uses that energy to build and repair itself.
items.why: Other strong answers: a cell works at body warmth, a cell controls how fast it goes, and a cell makes copies of itself.

items.p: Yeast, rice plants and people all break glucose down by the same first ten steps. What is the best explanation?
opts: They share an ancestor who had those steps
They copied the steps from each other
It is the only way sugar can ever break
items.why: The matching steps and matching enzymes are evidence that all three come from one early ancestor. Choosing 'the only way' is a fair thought, but some microbes break glucose down by other paths.

items.p: True or false: a growing child breaks the rule that things get more mixed up over time.
items.why: False. A body builds order inside only by giving out heat and waste, which add more disorder outside. Counting inside and outside together, the rule holds.

items.p: A lunch gives 600 kilocalories. Digesting and storing it costs about one tenth. How many kilocalories is that?
items.why: One tenth of 600 is 600 ÷ 10 = 60. So about 60 kilocalories are spent on handling the meal, and they end as heat.

items.p: Why does a cell break glucose down in many small steps and not in one big step?
opts: Small steps let it catch energy in ATP
One step would take too long
items.why: One big step would let all the energy out as heat at once, as a flame does. Small steps let the cell load ATP along the way.

items.p: The Hadza walk far every day, yet use about the same energy as office workers. Suggest one explanation.
items.a: The body may save energy on other jobs when a person is very active, so the daily total stays about the same.
items.why: This is Herman Pontzer's idea, and scientists still argue about it. Another fair answer is that the result depends on how body size is allowed for.

items.p: Sort these by whether they raise or lower a body's metabolic rate.
items.why: Working muscles, a meal, fever and cold all make cells break down more fuel. Sleep, torpor and a winter sleep all slow metabolism down.

items.p: Draw a mitochondrion inside a cell. Show what goes in and what comes out.
items.art: A blank cell outline with one large empty bean shape inside it.
items.a: A bean shape with a folded inner layer. Arrows in: pieces of glucose or fat, and oxygen. Arrows out: carbon dioxide, water, ATP and heat.
items.why: A strong drawing has oxygen going in. Leaving out oxygen suggests a mix-up with fermentation, which needs none.

items.p: In 1935, mice were fed fat that carried a label. Where did most of the label turn up?
opts: In the air they breathed out, at once
In the body fat of the mice
items.why: Most of the labelled fat was built into the body's own fat stores before being used. This showed that the body's stores are always being changed for new material.

items.p: Lynn Margulis showed that mitochondria were once free-living ____.
items.why: Mitochondria have their own ring of genes and divide by themselves, as bacteria do. Their genes match one group of bacteria.

items.p: Kleiber found that an animal 10,000 times heavier uses only about 1,000 times the energy. Give one idea scientists have for why.
items.a: A big body has less skin for its weight, so it loses less heat for each kilogram. Another idea is that longer blood vessels limit how fast fuel reaches each cell.
items.why: Either idea is a strong answer. The best answers add that scientists have not settled the question.

items.p: Put these in order of how much energy each uses for one kilogram of body in a day, from most to least.
items.why: Small warm animals use the most for their weight. A python does not keep a steady warmth, so they use the least.

items.p: True or false: brown fat cells break down fuel mainly to load ATP.
items.why: False. Brown fat cells let the energy out as heat without loading much ATP. That is how a newborn baby keeps warm without shivering.

items.p: Two scientists argue about how life began.

views.says: Metabolism came first. Chains of chemical changes ran in warm rock before any genes existed.
Genes came first. A molecule that could copy itself had to exist before anything else could last.

items.ask: Which idea seems more likely to you? Give your reason. Then say what the other side explains well.
items.a: A strong answer says what each view explains well, and admits that nobody knows yet. It may add that every cell today needs both.
items.why: Both are real ideas held by working scientists, and neither has been shown to be right.

items.p: A lotus flower stays near 32 degrees Celsius on a cool night. Where does the heat come from?
opts: The flower's cells breaking down stored food fast
items.why: Lotus cells break down stored food very quickly, and let the energy out as heat. Choosing 'stored sunlight' is close in one way: the food was made with sunlight, but the heat comes from breaking it down.

opts: Joining amino acids into muscle protein
Burning fat on a long walk
quiz.why: Anabolism joins small molecules into larger ones. The other three break molecules down, so they are catabolism.

quiz.p: Where do your cells get the energy to build new molecules?
opts: From the blanket around the body
quiz.why: Breaking food molecules down loads ATP, and building spends it. Oxygen helps to break food down, but oxygen is not the fuel.

quiz.p: Why are you warm even when you sleep?
opts: Your cells break down food all the time, and heat escapes
The bed stores heat for you
Your heart heats the blood like a stove
You stop losing heat at night
quiz.why: Every step of metabolism lets some energy escape as heat, and metabolism never stops. Choosing 'the bed' is the blanket mistake: bedding only slows the heat leaving.

quiz.p: Why do you feel a little warmer after a meal?
opts: Digesting and storing food uses extra energy
Food stays hot in the stomach for hours
Eating stops heat leaving the skin
The meal turns straight into heat
quiz.why: The body spends extra ATP on digesting, absorbing and storing the meal, and that ends as heat. This is the thermic effect of food.

quiz.p: In a resting adult, which uses more energy?
opts: The brain, liver, heart and kidneys together
quiz.why: Those four organs are about one twentieth of the body's weight and use more than half of its resting energy. Resting muscle uses little for its size.

opts: A gas that yeast give off
A store of glucose in the liver and muscles
quiz.why: Glycogen is many glucose units joined in a branching chain. It is the body's quick, small store of fuel.

quiz.p: When the body uses up stored fat, how does most of it leave?
opts: As carbon dioxide in the breath
quiz.why: The carbon atoms of the fat leave as carbon dioxide. Choosing 'as heat' mixes up energy with atoms. The energy leaves as heat, but the atoms leave as gas and water.

quiz.p: In the Yeast Fuel Test, why did one bottle have yeast but no food?
opts: To show the gas comes from breaking down food
To give the yeast a rest
quiz.why: That bottle is the comparison. It had the same yeast and water, so any extra gas in the other bottles must come from the food.

quiz.p: True or false: an adult who has stopped growing no longer builds new body material.
quiz.why: False. The body breaks down and rebuilds its own proteins and cells all the time. An adult rebuilds about 300 grams of protein a day.

applications: Bakers and idli makers control fermentation. They keep batter and dough warm so that yeast and bacteria break sugars down faster and give off more gas.
Doctors measure a patient's metabolic rate from the oxygen they breathe in and the carbon dioxide they breathe out. This tells a hospital how much food a very ill person needs.
People with diabetes measure the glucose in a drop of blood. The reading shows whether glucose is getting from the blood into the cells.
Sports scientists plan what runners and cyclists eat before and during a long race, so that their glycogen stores do not run out.
Nurses keep newborn babies warm against a parent's skin. This is called kangaroo care. A small baby loses heat fast and has little fuel to make more.
Vets and farmers give a newborn calf, kid or lamb the mother's first milk within hours of birth, so that the young animal has fuel to make heat.
Engineers who design the cooling for a cinema hall or a metro coach count the people, because each person adds about 80 to 100 watts of heat.
A PET scanner in a hospital shows which parts of a body are using the most glucose. Doctors use it to study the brain and to find tumours.

open_questions.q: Why does metabolic rate rise more slowly than body weight, from a shrew to an elephant?
open_questions.why_open: The pattern has been measured since 1932. Scientists have at least three explanations and have not agreed on one.

open_questions.q: When a person becomes much more active, does their body save energy somewhere else?
open_questions.why_open: Some measurements suggest that the daily total hardly rises. Others disagree, and it is hard to measure free-living people for months.

open_questions.q: Did metabolism begin before genes, or genes before metabolism?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody was there, and both ideas can explain some of the evidence. Laboratory tests of early-Earth chemistry are still going on.

open_questions.q: Why do animals with a slower metabolism for their size often live longer?
open_questions.why_open: The link is real across many mammals, but birds and bats break the pattern. Nobody knows the cause for certain.

open_questions.q: How does a hibernating bear live for months on body fat without losing much muscle?
open_questions.why_open: A person lying in bed that long would lose a lot of muscle. How the bear's cells keep rebuilding protein is still being worked out.

maths.problem: In a Yeast Fuel Test, the sugar balloon measured 12 centimetres round at 10 minutes, 18 at 20 minutes and 24 at 30 minutes. What would you predict for 40 minutes? Why can the pattern not go on for ever?
maths.answer: About 30 centimetres. The pattern must stop when the sugar runs out.
maths.explain: The balloon grows by 6 centimetres every 10 minutes: 12, 18, 24. The next number in the pattern is 24 + 6 = 30. The gas comes from breaking sugar down, and the bottle has only two teaspoons of sugar. When that is used up, no more gas is made.
maths.context: This is about the Yeast Fuel Test, where yeast in a bottle break sugar down and fill a balloon with gas. These are made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example: the sugar balloon over time

maths.why_maths: A pattern lets you predict the next measurement. Knowing the science tells you when the pattern must break.

maths.problem: The brain is about 2 parts in 100 of an adult's weight. It uses about 20 parts in 100 of the resting energy. For its weight, how many times the body's average does the brain use?
maths.explain: If every part used energy in step with its weight, 2 parts in 100 of the body would use 2 parts in 100 of the energy. The brain uses 20 parts. 20 ÷ 2 = 10. So each gram of brain uses about 10 times as much energy as an average gram of body.
maths.context: This is about Twenty Beans, where 20 beans stand for the energy a resting adult uses and you place them on the parts of a body.
maths.why_maths: Comparing a part's share of the energy with its share of the weight shows which parts work hardest for their size.

maths.problem: A lunch gives 600 kilocalories. The body spends about one tenth of that on digesting and storing the meal. How much is spent, and how much is left for everything else?
maths.answer: About 60 kilocalories are spent, and about 540 are left.
maths.explain: One tenth of 600 is 600 ÷ 10 = 60. Then 600 − 60 = 540. The 60 kilocalories end as heat within a few hours, which is one reason you feel warmer after a meal.
maths.context: This is about the Lunch Test, where you measure your pulse and temperature before and after a meal.
maths.why_maths: A fraction of the meal's energy tells you the size of the after-meal heat, which is too small to see on a thermometer.

maths.problem: A resting ten-year-old gives out heat at about 55 watts. About how much heat do 30 resting children give out together? Is that more or less than a 1,500 watt room heater?
maths.answer: About 1,650 watts, a little more than the room heater.
maths.explain: 30 × 55 = 1,650. A room heater gives 1,500 watts, and 1,650 is more than 1,500. So a classroom of 30 children warms the room about as much as one room heater left on all day.
maths.context: This is about Warmer Than the Room, where a tumbler of warm water went cool and you stayed warm, because your body makes heat all the time.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying one body's heat by the number of people explains why a crowded room or bus gets warm.

maths.problem: When a body uses up stored fat, 84 parts in every 100 leave as carbon dioxide in the breath. The rest leave as water. If 500 grams of fat are used up, how many grams leave in the breath as carbon dioxide?
maths.explain: 84 parts in 100 of 500 grams is 500 × 84 ÷ 100 = 420 grams. The other 80 grams leave as water.
maths.context: This is about One Idli's Journey, where you draw the roads that food molecules take in your cells, and where their atoms end up.
maths.why_maths: Working out the share shows that most of a used-up store leaves through the lungs, which few people would guess.

maths.problem: In a Lunch Test, Kavya's pulse counts before lunch were 76 and 80. Thirty minutes after lunch they were 86 and 90. What is the mean of each pair? By how many beats did her pulse rise?
maths.answer: The means are 78 and 88. Her pulse rose by 10 beats a minute.
maths.explain: Before lunch: 76 + 80 = 156, and 156 ÷ 2 = 78. After lunch: 86 + 90 = 176, and 176 ÷ 2 = 88. The rise is 88 − 78 = 10 beats a minute.
maths.context: This is about the Lunch Test, where you count your pulse twice before lunch and twice after it. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: One count can be off by a few beats. The mean of two counts is a number you can trust more.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that the body rebuilds itself all the time? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: A hundred years ago, most scientists pictured the body as an engine. Food was the fuel. The body burned it straight away, and the engine's own parts stayed in place until they wore out. Nobody could test this, because an atom from food looks the same as an atom already in the body. Then, in 1932, Harold Urey found deuterium. It is a heavy kind of hydrogen, and it can be told apart from ordinary hydrogen. Rudolf Schoenheimer had left Germany in 1933 and worked at Columbia University in New York. With David Rittenberg he made fat that carried deuterium as a label, and in 1935 they fed it to mice. If the old idea was right, the mice would burn the fat and the label would leave. Instead, most of the label turned up in the body fat of the mice. Later they labelled amino acids with a heavy kind of nitrogen and fed them to adult rats. The label appeared in the rats' own proteins, though the rats were not growing. So the body was taking itself apart and rebuilding itself all the time.
how_we_found_out.who: Rudolf Schoenheimer and David Rittenberg, with Harold Urey, who found deuterium
how_we_found_out.when: 1932 (deuterium found), 1935 (the first tests with labelled fat) and 1942 (Schoenheimer's book, The Dynamic State of Body Constituents)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the body is like an engine: food is burned straight away as fuel, and the body's own material stays in place for years. Labelled atoms showed that food atoms are built into the body within days, and that the body's own material is broken down and rebuilt all the time.
how_we_found_out.art: A laboratory bench in the 1930s with two mice in a cage and a dish of food, and a drawing showing marked atoms from the food appearing inside the outline of a mouse.

roots.context: We have learned that cells break food down for energy, build the body up with that energy, and give off heat at every step. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Yeast Fuel Test, the yeast who were given sugar made gas and froth, and the yeast with no food made almost none. Like yeast, your cells can build only with energy they get by breaking food down. Each time, part of that energy escapes as heat. So your body is built by breaking food apart, and your warmth shows that this is happening now.
deep_truth.habit: We think of breaking down and building up as opposites, and we call one decay and the other growth. In your cells they are two halves of one exchange, and the building cannot happen without the breaking. We also think the body has a heater somewhere. Nearly all of its heat is simply what escapes each time a cell passes energy on.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Yeast Fuel Test, only the bottles where yeast could break a food down filled their balloons. In Grown in the Dark, a moong seedling built a root and a shoot while the food store in the seed leaves shrank. In Warmer Than the Room, the water cooled and you did not.

three.who_am_i: The material of your body is changed for new material from food all the time. What lasts is the way you are built, and the life that keeps rebuilding it.
three.what_is_life: To be alive is to break down and build up at the same time, without stopping. A yeast cell does it, a lotus does it, and you do it.
three.what_is_this_world: The energy that warms your cheek came to the Earth as sunlight. A plant stored it, you used it, and it leaves you as heat. You are one place it passes through.

roots.thread: Sunlight is one kind of energy. A rice plant stores it in starch. Your cells break the starch down, and the same energy becomes a heartbeat, a thought, a new patch of skin and the warmth of your hand. Then it all leaves you as heat. Awareness, the ground that everything rises from, shows itself here as one energy taking many forms in turn. None of the energy is used up. It is only passed on.

teachings.teaching: Bhrigu's father tells him to find out for himself what all beings come from. Bhrigu thinks hard, and his first answer is food. Beings are born from food, they live by food, and when they die they go back into food. His father sends him to think further.
teachings.link: The science of metabolism says the same about the body. It is built from food, kept alive by food, and returns to the food of other beings. The Upanishad treats this as a true first answer, and then asks what lies beyond it.

teachings.teaching: The Greek thinker Heraclitus said that this world was made by no god and no person. It always was and will be an ever-living fire, being kindled in measures and going out in measures.
teachings.link: A living body is like this in a plain way. Breaking down and building up go on together, in measured amounts, and the body keeps its form only while both continue.

science.text: Energy is never made or destroyed in a living body. What goes in as food comes out as heat, work or stored material (measured by Atwater and Rosa in the 1890s).
The molecules of a body are broken down and rebuilt all the time, so the body's material is always changing while its form stays (Schoenheimer, 1930s).
Life may have begun as a simple metabolism, a chain of chemical changes in warm rock, before there were any genes. Other scientists think genes came first.

other_view.who: The Charvaka school of ancient India, as reported by Madhava in the Sarvadarshanasamgraha
other_view.view: The Charvakas said that awareness is not the ground of anything. It appears when the elements come together in a body. In the same way, the power to make a person drunk appears when grain and a starter are mixed and left to ferment, though neither had that power alone. On this view, a mind is something a metabolism produces, and it ends when the body ends.

practice.title: Feel your own warmth
practice.say: Sit still and rub nothing. Hold your open palms close to your cheeks without touching them. Wait, and feel the warmth that crosses the gap. This heat is leaving you all the time. It came from the food you ate today. Before that it was sunlight on a field. Now breathe out slowly onto your palm. That breath carries carbon atoms from the same food. Sit for five slow breaths and notice the warmth and the breath leaving.
practice.kid: Sit still. Hold your palms near your cheeks. Do not touch. Feel the warmth cross the gap. That heat came from your food. Breathe out slowly on your palm. Your breath carries atoms from your food. Take five slow breaths.

ask: Your body is built by breaking food apart. Is breaking down a bad thing, a good thing, or neither?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, project and challenge was reasoned through step by step, as a parent and child would do it in a city flat. None of them has been tried at home yet, so treat the expected results as likely, not certain. The Yeast Fuel Test (core) needs dry yeast and balloons, which most homes must buy. Old yeast or hot water gives no froth, and the step says to start again. Sugar should give a firm balloon in 20 to 30 minutes. Atta usually gives a little gas, because flour holds a little sugar. Warmer Than the Room (core) needs only a tumbler of warm water and a 30 minute wait, which the yeast test fills. The Lunch Test asks a child to eat lunch about 75 minutes late on the second day. The change in pulse is usually clear, and the change in temperature is usually too small to see. Both outcomes are said honestly in the steps. In Hold It at 37, a fever thermometer is slow, taking up to a minute for each reading, so a kitchen thermometer is easier. A grown-up handles all hot water. In Grown in the Dark, moong sprout reliably, but rinse them daily or they turn sour. Budget Day was played through on paper for two players: a game takes about 20 minutes and uses about 100 beans for two players. Facts and numbers were looked up while writing: the Schoenheimer and Cori histories, the python, lotus, shrew and honey bee figures, the brain's share of a child's energy, the fat-to-breath figures, the cost of digesting a meal and the advice on warming a newborn kid. The title and channel of each video were confirmed through YouTube's public lookup. The videos themselves were not watched.
